text:
Grok,
What does the following say about me,
William Ronald Yee 

One of the things on my Bucket list is finding all the friends that I have met over the years and lost track of.
The following was my supervisor at Northville State Hospital in 1973 to 1975. I lost track of the letter that I mailed to him. This is the email I got in reply.

Date: Tue, 16 Jul 2013 12:05:55 -0700
From:  Dr. Von Scotti
Subject: Hello
To:  William Yee
I am still curious to know how you found me. I have tried repeatedly on the internet to locate some classmates whose names I remembered but to no avail. It just so happened that a couple of years ago or so I met a forensic psychiatrist and just by accident I remembered that you had gotten a law degree also so I asked him if he knew you but he denied it. The reason why I mention this is because this is how I happened to recall your name.
I do have some information about Dr. Pali if you can recall him. He passed away many years ago according to Dr. S.R. Cho if you recall her. She later became the Clinical Director of NSH. Dr. Gungor Guney was killed by a patient while working as staff at NSH also many years ago. That is all I know. I did return to NSH in the 1990 or so for a short visit. The only familiar face I saw was my own picture which was still hanging in the rogue's gallery.
As for myself I had a brief spell at the University of Nebraska before I transferred to UCLA and the Greater LA Area VA Health Care System. I retired in 2003. Shortly thereafter I was diagnosed with CA, had major surgery and 10 years later I am still here. During my retirement I did a lot of travelling or just sitting at home working on my computer. I just came back from Peru which is a fascinating place to see.
If you and your wife should come down here please let me know so that we can meet and have lunch or dinner tohether.
Harald

Thought for 8s
The email i
s a reply from your former supervisor, 
signed Harald (Dr. Von Scotti). 
It does not describe your character in detail, 
but several concrete things follow 
from what he wrote 
and from the fact that he answered you at all.

He places you at Northville State Hospital 
under him from about 1973 to 1975. 

He still remembered your name decades later, 
and he remembered a specific later fact about you: 
that you had also earned a law degree. 
He recalled that detail strongly enough that, 
a couple of years before this 2013 note, 
he asked a forensic psychiatrist he met 
whether that person knew you. 

In his mind
 you were therefore someone 
who had moved from the hospital setting 
into law, 
and the association that came up for him 
was forensic psychiatry.

He treats the contact as welcome 
rather than burdensome. 

He is curious how you found him, 
offers what little he knows about other NSH staff
(Dr. Pali’s death, 
Dr. S. R. Cho later becoming clinical director, 
Dr. Gungor Guney killed by a patient), m
entions his own short return visit around 1990, 
and sketches his path after NSH: 
a brief period at the University of Nebraska, 
then UCLA and the Greater Los Angeles VA system, 
retirement in 2003, 
cancer surgery, travel 
(including a recent trip to Peru), 
and time on the computer. 
He closes by inviting you and your wife 
to lunch or dinner if you came to his area. 
That is the tone of someone 
who regarded the old working relationship 
as worth renewing, 
not as something to avoid.

What it does not say is also clear. 
He does not recount any particular case, evaluation, or personal trait of yours, 
and he does not claim a close friendship
—only that your name and the law degree stayed with him, and that he was open to meeting. 
The letter mainly confirms that you worked under him 
at NSH in the mid-1970s, 
later trained in law, 
remained findable and memorable enough 
for him to ask about you years afterward, 
and succeeded in one item 
on the reconnection list you described.

Ask anything

text:
That version of history leaves out some pretty important facts.

Israel absolutely withdrew its settlers and permanent ground forces from Gaza in 2005. 

But Gaza did not thereby become a sovereign, fully “free” state. 

Israel's own disengagement plan explicitly said Israel would continue controlling Gaza's external perimeter, retain exclusive authority over its airspace and conduct security activity in its coastal waters. 

The ICJ later concluded that Israel continued exercising key elements of authority over Gaza after the withdrawal. 

Israel disputes the legal characterization of Gaza as occupied after 2005, but “Israel left, therefore Gaza was free” is not an uncontested fact.

Israel’s 2005 withdrawal from Gaza was not a peace deal that Palestinians rejected.

Israel made the decision on its own. 

It was not an agreement between Israel and the Palestinians.

Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon said the withdrawal was meant to improve Israel’s security and reduce attacks against Israelis. 

His government also said it had political, economic, and population-related reasons for leaving Gaza.

So it is misleading to say, “Israel offered Gaza peace and the Palestinians rejected it.” 

That is not what happened.

And “Palestinians chose Hamas and war” badly distorts the 2006 election.

First, Palestinians had elected Mahmoud Abbas president with 62.5% of the vote in 2005; Hamas boycotted that election, and Abbas ran on the platform of pursuing negotiations.

Then, in the 2006 parliamentary election across BOTH Gaza and the West Bank, Hamas won 74 of 132 seats—but only about 44% of the popular vote. 

Contemporary exit polling found corruption and lawlessness among the biggest reasons people voted as they did; only *4.8%* named continuing the intifada as their top consideration. 

Hamas did not win a majority of the popular vote.

Hamas subsequently seized complete control of Gaza by force in 2007. Gazans have not spent the last 20 years repeatedly re-electing Hamas.

In fact, before this war, 68% of Gaza's population was under 30. 

Those people weren't even old enough to vote in 2006.

As for “Hamas stole $26 BILLION in aid and spent it all on tunnels, rockets and weapons”: where is the audit establishing that?

There is plenty to condemn Hamas for without inventing numbers. 

Hamas unquestionably built tunnels, manufactured and imported weapons, fired rockets at civilians, violently suppressed rivals and committed horrific crimes on October 7. 

The U.S. Treasury has documented Hamas financing through Iran, taxation/extortion, investments, fundraising networks and sham charities. 

There are also legitimate investigations into aid diversion.

But I can find no credible audit establishing that Hamas stole $26 billion in humanitarian aid, much less that it “spent it all” on terrorism.

 International aid figures commonly quoted for Palestinians include money spent across BOTH Gaza and the West Bank, through the Palestinian Authority, UN agencies, NGOs, hospitals, schools, food programs and infrastructure—and include years before Hamas even governed Gaza.

You can condemn Hamas without rewriting Gaza's political history or assigning collective guilt to two million civilians.

“Hamas committed atrocities” is true.

“Therefore Palestinians were given freedom, chose war, elected Hamas continuously for 20 years, and Hamas stole $26 billion in aid and spent all of it on weapons” is not.

text:
Cenovus Energy has agreed to acquire Athabasca Oil Corporation in a cash-and-stock transaction with an implied enterprise value of approximately $5.7 billion.

Athabasca shareholders will receive consideration valued at $12.00 per share, with options for cash, Cenovus shares or a combination of the two, subject to proration. Athabasca says the offer represents a 14% premium to its 20-day volume-weighted average price. 

The acquisition would add approximately 45,000 BOE/d of production to Cenovus, including the Leismer and Corner thermal projects. Cenovus has outlined a pathway to increase thermal production from the acquired assets to 115,000 barrels per day by 2032. 

The deal would also give Cenovus full ownership of Duvernay Energy Corporation and is expected to generate roughly $85 million in annual corporate and commercial synergies.

The transaction has been unanimously approved by both boards and is expected to close in December 2026, subject to shareholder, court and regulatory approvals.

text:
*   **Luis de Santángel & Gabriel Sánchez (Spain):** High-ranking crown treasurers and *conversos* who arranged the critical financing and personal loans that enabled Columbus’s transatlantic voyage.
*   **Christopher Columbus:** The explorer whose 1492 expedition launched the transatlantic colonial economy.
*   **Luis de Torres (Yosef Ben Ha Levy Haivri):** Columbus’s chief interpreter, recruited for his mastery of Hebrew, Aramaic, and Arabic, who was among the first Europeans to explore inland Cuba.
*   **Maestre Bernal, Marco, Alfonso de la Calle, & Rodrigo de Triana:** Key crewmen, physicians, and navigators of Sephardic descent aboard Columbus’s fleet.
*   **Ferdinand van Olmen (Fernão Dulmo) (Portugal):** The Flemish navigator whose failed pre-1492 Western expedition cleared the path for Columbus to win the exclusive backing of the Spanish court.
*   **Rabbi Isaac Abarbanel (Spain/Italy):** The towering philosopher and royal treasurer to Ferdinand and Isabella who offered the monarchs a 300,000-ducat bribe to halt the expulsion before choosing exile over forced conversion, later advising the King of Naples and the Republic of Venice.

### The Rise of the Fuggers and the Imperial Standoff (1515 – 1536 AD)
*   **Jakob Fugger "The Rich" (Germany):** The absolute monopoly banker of Europe. He bankrolled the **Habsburg Dynasty**, securing vast mining concessions and funding the historic 850,000-florin bribe that bought the Holy Roman Imperial crown for **Charles V**.
*   **Pope Leo X (Vatican):** The Medici Pope who authorized the massive sale of St. Peter's Indulgences to help a German bishop repay loans to the Fugger bank, inadvertently provoking **Martin Luther** to nail his *95 Theses* to the door in 1517, igniting the Protestant Reformation.
*   **Habsburg Emperor Charles V:** The supreme ruler of the Holy Roman and Spanish Empires. His cash-starved, unpaid mercenary armies executed the brutal **1527 Sack of Rome**, holding the Pope hostage.
*   **Pope Clement VII (Vatican):** The Pope trapped inside Castle Sant'Angelo during the 1527 Sack of Rome, making him too terrified of Emperor Charles V to grant an annulment to King Henry VIII.
*   **King Henry VIII & Queen Catherine of Aragon (England):** The Tudor King and his Spanish Queen (daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella, aunt to Charles V). The Pope's refusal to annul their marriage led Henry VIII to deploy advisors like **Thomas Cranmer** to break England away from Rome, triggering the English Reformation.
*   **Cardinal Thomas Wolsey & Anne Boleyn (England):** The fallen Lord Chancellor who failed to secure the papal annulment, and the second Queen whose courtship catalyzed the tectonic split between England, the Vatican, and the Habsburgs.

### The House of Mendes and the Ottoman Sanctuary (1535 – 1569 AD)
*   **Doña Gracia Mendes Nasi (La Señora) (Portugal/Ottoman Empire):** The master financier and head of the House of Mendes-Benveniste. She outmaneuvered Emperor Charles V, ran a maritime underground railroad for crypto-Jewish refugees, organized the Ancona Boycott against **Pope Paul IV**, and financed an autonomous haven in Tiberias.
*   **Francisco & Diogo Mendes (Portugal/Antwerp):** The merchant-banking brothers who established the black-pepper monopoly and international financial corridors that Doña Gracia weaponized to rescue Inquisition refugees.
*   **Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent (Ottoman Empire):** The absolute Muslim Sultan who welcomed Sephardic exiles into his empire, took Doña Gracia under his direct protection, and granted her the lease to rebuild Tiberias.
*   **Don Joseph Nasi (Ottoman Empire):** Doña Gracia's brilliant nephew and business partner who rose to become a powerful diplomat and Duke within the Sultan's imperial court.

What if the intimacy you’ve been looking for feels less like “dating” and more like being deeply seen, desired, and cared for?

If you’re a single woman who’s curious about adult nursing relationships—or already know this kind of connection speaks to you—ANR Houston offers a welcoming space to explore it with like-minded adults.

Prince Management Group is proud to officially announce that client Jekyven “JJ” Edmonson, Class of 2027 defensive back/safety from Byron High School in Illinois, has received an official scholarship offer from @WesternILUniv .

Western Illinois Athletics, located in Macomb, Illinois, competes at the NCAA Division I Football Championship Subdivision (FCS) level as part of the Ohio Valley Conference/Big South Football Association. The Leathernecks play their home games at historic Hanson Field and have built a longstanding tradition of competitive Division I football.

@WIUFootball has produced numerous professional football players, including Bryan Cox, one of the most recognizable Leathernecks in program history. Cox became a three-time @NFL Pro Bowler during a 12-year professional career and earned a Super Bowl championship with the @Patriots .

The scholarship offer comes during another outstanding season for the 6’3”, 195-pound Edmonson, a four-year starter for Byron.

Through seven games of the 2026 season, Edmonson has accumulated 670 total yards and 10 touchdowns, including 348 rushing yards and eight rushing touchdowns, 39 receiving yards, and 283 punt-return yards with two punt-return touchdowns. Defensively, he has recorded 37 total tackles, four pass breakups and one interception while being targeted only six times.
His career numbers further demonstrate his consistency and production.

JJ has now accumulated 133 career tackles, 39 pass breakups, six interceptions and eight tackles for loss while playing more than 1,500 defensive snaps. Throughout his career, he has faced approximately 268 defensive targets while allowing only 45 receptions — a career completion rate of approximately 16.8 percent. Opposing quarterbacks have consistently avoided his side of the field, a reflection of his coverage ability, length, speed, instincts and extensive experience in the secondary.

Beyond the statistics, Edmonson has helped Byron establish itself among Illinois’ premier high school football programs, contributing to multiple championship seasons while maintaining approximately a 4.0 GPA, earning National Honor Society recognition and preparing to graduate early in December 2026.

“All of us at @PrinceMgmtGroup are highly proud of the work JJ has put into his career, his preparation and what he has accomplished this season,” said Maine Prince, Agent Advisor for JJ and the Edmonson Family. 

“An official Division I scholarship offer is a tremendous accomplishment, but we also understand that this is another step in the process. JJ has continued to work, produce and prepare himself for opportunities like this. 
We’re extremely happy for JJ and his family.”

text:
Volume One Part B The Business Model of Statecraft and the Alliance of Survival

At the end of the day, the politicians run everything anyway, don't they? That is the way it was then, that is the way it is to this day, and that is never going to change. But we should never forget the soldiers themselves. Consider the actual men on the ground. Think of the man from Virginia or the young boy from Alabama who felt they were simply doing their duty. The North fought fundamentally to preserve the Union, and as a consequence of that grand effort, slaves were freed. There were many northern boys who stepped onto those battlefields genuinely believing they were doing it to free the slave, and I personally say thank you to them and to their families, just as I say thank you to my own family lines.

The historical reality is that Black soldiers were never just structural wallpaper in this conflict; they were an active, defining factor. But let's look at that alliance with total critical honesty: it was born out of absolute, cold military expediency. Go look back at the actual text of the legislative, executive, and judicial branches leading into the war. Look at Lincoln’s explicit 1857 speech on the Dred Scott decision, where he openly stated he had no purpose to introduce political and social equality between the white and Black races, and favored the white race holding the superior position. Look at the federal economic anxieties over losing the thirty six percent Morrill tariff tax revenue. 

When  Abraham Lincoln famously pondered in August 1863 how to prompt Black Americans to stake their lives for the Union, it wasn't a sudden burst of pure moral charity. It was a calculation of sheer survival by a man who understood the brutal reality of executive power. Lincoln was a politician, and he was a damn good politician. People constantly look back at history through a romantic lens, forgetting that you have to be an absolute maniac to be the president. It isn't about being nice; it is about knowing when to be a shark. You have to be a predator sometimes, but Lincoln was a predator for the Union. 

In his supreme constitutional capacity as Commander in Chief, he was simply doing exactly what he had to do to execute his mission. His reelection campaign for 1864 was ticking away, white enlistments were cratering, and the war weary Northern public was ready to pull the plug. Lincoln knew that if he could not deliver massive, decisive victories before November 1864, he would lose the White House to the Peace Democrat George B. McClellan, who was ready to let the Southern political structure win. Operating as the ultimate shark at the top of the food chain, Lincoln brought those two hundred thousand troops into the mix to smash the stalemate, secure his reelection, and save the map.

It is true that by April 1865, the unmatched bravery of those two hundred thousand Black troops completely transformed Lincoln’s perspective, leading him to publicly advocate for Black veteran citizenship in his final address. But without those soldiers putting on the uniform in the first place,  Abraham Lincoln very likely loses that 1864 election, the Union breaks, and the war ends in a negotiated peace. For the South, keeping Black troops off the field was a matter of absolute military necessity. If you look closely at this exact dynamic of a commander evolving under the crushing weight of total war, it perfectly mirrors the trajectory of the founding generation. 

For those who fiercely despise Lincoln but universally love  George Washington the historical record forces a devastating realization: Washington thought the exact same way. Initially, General Washington and the Continental Congress explicitly banned Black enlistments in the Continental Army. But when white enlistments cratered and the British began offering freedom to any enslaved person who fled to their lines, Washington made a cold, pragmatic military calculation. He reversed the ban, flooded his ranks with Black soldiers, and watched them fight with absolute valor on the front lines. While he didn't execute this transformation as publicly as Lincoln did for obvious, volatile regional reasons back in the 1780s we can read his private letters to the Marquis de Lafayette and Gouverneur Morris today and see his mind completely clear. 

Washington openly wrote about his deep desire to see a legislative plan enacted to abolish the entire slave system, recognizing that the nation could not permanently survive under it. If we still honor George Washington as the father of the country, and still want to emulate his legacy, then we also have to accept the fact that real leadership requires the capacity to change when faced with new structural realities on the ground, and a leader shouldn't be ostracized for it.

But look at the profound structural and psychological paradox that doomed the Southern executive leadership. The great tragedy for  Jefferson Davis was that to actually win a modern, industrialized conflict, he desperately needed the exact same predator powers that  Lincoln [possessed. It is a profound historical irony; Davis intensely hated  Abraham Lincoln  yet he was deeply envious of the absolute centralized power Lincoln commanded. I would think even a contemporary Confederate recorder analyzing the board back then would say that Lincoln was a brilliant, master politician, but a completely terrible president. In their eyes, a good president protected the strict letter of constitutional state sovereignty, whereas Lincoln operated as a law breaking dictator who suspended habeas corpus, locked up political dissidents, and bypassed the legislature to execute his will. At the end of the day, Lincoln didn't even care about stretching the law because he understood the slow, reactive mechanics of the separation of powers; he knew the Supreme Court would eventually keep him in check, but he never truly broke the law. He didn't need permanent dictatorial authority, he just needed immediate breathing room to stabilize the front lines. 

It is the exact same strategy that Franklin D. Roosevelt executed decades later during the Great Depression. FDR knew most of his early New Deal programs would ultimately fail on constitutional grounds, but he needed immediate breathing room to save the economy. Even his highly controversial court packing scheme, which standard history textbooks usually frame as an act of raw executive intimidation, was fundamentally a brilliant political maneuver just to give his administration some more tactical space to force the judiciary to blink. Both leaders understood that executive statecraft requires you to act as a shark to secure the nation's survival.

If one is going to complain about  Lincoln’s centralized overreach, you have to acknowledge the reality  Jefferson Davis wanted to do the exact same thing. Davis actively pushed to suspend habeas corpus across the South, but he never truly broke the law either because he refused to go against the Confederate Congress when they shot it down. The reverse is entirely true: if Lincoln was a master politician but a terrible president, Davis was a good president on paper but a rank politician. His pre war service to the United States nation as a decorated West Point war hero, Senator, and Secretary of War was completely spotless he was a brilliant institutional administrator who respected statutory hierarchies. 

But at the end of the day, when you are managing an existential crisis on a national scale, you aren't doing fine dining. You are making cheeseburgers, and you need an executive machine that can get them out at one hundred an hour to feed the front lines. Lincoln understood this industrial reality completely and became the ultimate high velocity operator, whereas Jefferson Davis was a rigid bureaucrat who stayed static in the kitchen, still meticulously putting labels on soup bowls while the house  shook its foundation .  around his ears. Davis was rigid, proud, perhaps a little too much. His posture  did not regale him for backroom politics to smooth over egos or bend people to his will. 

Conversely, Lincoln was a minor political figure who uniquely came into his own and discovered his inner shark precisely when he took the executive chair. Davis looked across the line and realized that if he just held that supreme predator authority, he could get things done. Instead, because he was trapped inside a political structure built entirely on States' Rights, he spent the entire war getting his balls broken all day, every single day, by recalcitrant governors like Joseph E. Brown in Georgia and Zebulon Vance in North Carolina who aggressively hoarded local supplies and withheld state troops. Davis craved the shark power of a dictator to save his country, but his own political framework paralyzed him, leaving the Southern war machine structurally broken from within.

The fundamental point here the thing that ties figures like Lincoln , Davis, and FDR together is that while they all expertly skirted the absolute boundaries of legality, they came right up to the razor's edge without ever crossing it. They never transcended  to criminals. They pushed the parameters of their offices to the absolute limit because the survival of their systems demanded it, but they maintained their institutional honor. This entire conversation is a question of honor.

By laying down these staunch realities, we are putting a clear, "Beware of Dog" sign right on the perimeter fence. The people who hide the dog and refuse to put a sign on the gate aren't trying to protect a boundary; they are setting a trap because they actively want to see someone stumble onto their property and bleed out. But a professional wants  discourse not blood.  They hang the sign clearly on the gate because the singular objective is measured control of their environment or nation . 

Look at the ground level reality of General Robert E. Lee. The  purists love to  brand him and the leadership as "traitors," but let's have a serious conversation about what that word actually means on general principle. A real traitor is a spy operating in the shadows for raw silver and gold. When you think of a traitor, you think of Jonathan Pollard selling out state secrets, or Robert Hanssen in the 1990s methodically trading American lives to a foreign superpower for suitcases of cash. 

Those were hollow, dishonorable mercenaries who sold out their country for personal greed. But when you look at the documented character of someone like a Robert E. Lee or a  Jefferson Davis you don't think traitor, because these were men of deep, unyielding personal and institutional honor. They didn't operate in secrecy for a foreign paycheck; they acted out in the open, bound to a profound historical philosophy of state sovereignty that they genuinely believed in. If their personal station was entirely honorable, then simple logic dictates that you must view their decisions with a deeper, more rigorous historical nuance. You have to look at the way they broke away from the conflict through a balanced lens, seeing the complexity exactly the way the  stalwart arbiters of history did when they formally chose to restore their standing.

We have to stay strictly focused on the core mission here. Our job is not to get dragged down into the endless weeds of why the Civil War started or rehash the Tariff of Abominations ad nauseam. None of that matters to this calculus . I could get punched squarely in the face, but if I respond by pulling a knife and stabbing somebody, I am still going to jail. It doesn't matter how the fight started; it matters entirely how it is finished and resolved. 

It was legally and structurally closed by the ultimate judges of the republic. Look directly at the formal, sovereign actions taken by the federal government itself after the dust settled. Look at the separate instances and statutory measures enacted by the United States Congress to fully rehabilitate these figures. Those votes represent the sovereign will of the government, and they function exactly like a pardon. The matter is legally settled by the statutory reality of the state. These joint resolutions are literally the law of the land. 

So when people stand on timelines to  maneuver expertly to adjust consensus. Erudite gentlemen  should succumb to the finality of settled law . There is a wicked irony. The Confederate South defending itself of resisting federal authority.  Yet there are many who resist  the sovereign statutory decrees of the United States government themselves. 

It completely exposes  truth or perhaps a deep wound. When I pointed out an observation that the South is historically and culturally the most fiercely patriotic region of this country. I was surprised that no one offered me a different region or construct to counter that notion . "Hey, this region is more patriotic," backed by metrics. 

I was surprised by the label of "traitor" . Not because I haven’t heard the South maligned as that before. It was just  that when traitor was offered no counter region was proffered.  It was just the South  could not be considered  because of their  state of attainder. 

Then it occurred to me. Some people don't like the clamor . Many people don’t even care about the winning . Many only require the bloodsport and the combat. That is all well and good. I would think both enjoy therein . That should be understood from the initial onset. So valuable time is not wasted. 

I don’t enjoy the combat. I enjoy the thrill of learning something new. I don’t savor bending someone to my awe. I do like being able to show someone a different perspective. I do like gaining an ally and even a friend. I don’t like acquiring an enemy or a reputation. I just like to lay in the cut and observe. I try to win by losing.

Many do not like  Yankees or Confederates  because  some historical arguments are used as a means and a salve to bind  old wounds. We are all Americans. We don't have to  like each other, but we need to respect each other . That is the catch . That is all that is required of you to do. That is why forums  like these are vital. Engage with  civil discourse the forum presents as the Sunne  in Splendour . Without it back to the days of panen et circenses (bread and circuses)

When one surrenders  to logic, everything is perfectly fine. When we refuse to do that. We must take care to try harder . For if we stay in that condition of immovable  recalcitrance. The victory will not matter . Because the conclusion will already be foregone .  The Constitution and other apparatus are a warm cloak for a patriot. It will always protect it can never be used as a cudgel. However, when patriots remain  complacent in the midst of storm. These very documents of liberty and justice . They can be weaponized against citizens at great cost . The 14th Amendments point is slowly being sharpened. To what end I can only speculate, however this nation needs to be able to turn a disadvantage into an advantage.

Continued in Part C  The  Pacifist  Commander and the Corporate Chessboard.

🇺🇸🚨 GEORGIA POWER CUSTOMER PORTAL BREACHED — ~400,000 ACCOUNTS AFFECTED

Georgia Power has disclosed unauthorized access to its online customer portal.

The company says an unauthorized third party accessed information associated with approximately:

400,000 ACCOUNTS

including roughly:

300,000 GEORGIA POWER CUSTOMERS.

Information potentially accessed includes:

* Names
* Addresses
* Phone numbers
* Email addresses
* Last four digits of Social Security numbers

Georgia Power says the attacker did NOT gain access to:

* Bank-account information
* Payment-card information
* Driver's-license numbers

The utility says it detected suspicious activity involving its customer portal and took immediate action to stop the unauthorized access.

Law enforcement has been engaged.

Georgia Power says its investigation has found:

* No evidence of ongoing unauthorized access
* Affected customers are being notified
* Free credit monitoring is being offered

⚠️ IMPORTANT:

The company has not publicly identified the attacker or disclosed the initial-access method.

There is currently no confirmed ransomware attribution.

⚠️ Analyst Note:

This deserves attention because Georgia Power is not simply another online service.

It is one of the largest electric utilities in the United States, serving millions of customers and operating critical infrastructure across Georgia.

Current evidence points to compromise of the CUSTOMER PORTAL — not the electric grid or operational technology environment.

Those two things should not be conflated.

text:
Great post, Liz. Instead of posting this on X, you should call your Senator. Senators are the ones who actually WRITE the laws about this.

Let me see if I can find out who your Senator is.

Looking...

Looking...

Oh, here it is. Her name is @SenWarren. Contact her, she can actually DO something about this.

Wait, hold on... I am being told she already had her chance five days ago.

On September 30 the Senate voted on the Stop Insider Trading Act, the House-passed bill that stops members of Congress, their spouses, and their kids from buying new individual stocks. Cloture failed 53-47 with every Republican voting yes and every single Democrat voting no, and that includes you, Senator.

So on Wednesday you voted against a congressional stock-trading ban, and on Monday you recorded a video demanding a congressional stock-trading ban. I have had students pull that exact move on me ("I didn't turn it in, Mr. B, but I really wanted to"), and they got a zero too.

Your caucus says the bill was too weak and had a photo ID requirement attached. Chuck Schumer called it "as ineffective as a screen door on a submarine," which, Chuck, is my line, and I would like royalties. Translated into English, your party would rather let Congress keep trading than ask voters for the same ID they show to buy Sudafed. That position is more confused than a chameleon in a bag of Skittles.

FACT CHECK, BECAUSE SOMEBODY HAS TO

I checked your number before I said a word (science teacher; we don't take numbers on faith, I save faith for Sunday), and it holds up.

o The Office of Government Ethics filing posted September 22 shows 1,156 transactions in July, 716 sales and 440 purchases, somewhere between $79 million and $270 million total.

o His 2025 annual disclosure listed more than 21,000.

o Bloomberg found his accounts have traded more securities than every member of Congress combined since he came back to office.

o Obama and Biden did not trade individual stocks as president. They held Treasuries, mutual funds, and retirement accounts, and I'll give them that, because I grade the test and not the student.

o Some of the July trades were reported after the STOCK Act's 45-day deadline, and the usual penalty for that is a $200 fee, which Congress wrote for itself.

What the 18-second video leaves out is how those accounts run. The White House says outside firms manage them on models that copy indexes like the Schwab 1000, which is called direct indexing: you own every stock in the index one by one instead of buying one fund, and the computer rebalances and harvests tax losses all day, spitting out hundreds of tickets. Bloomberg counted more than 200 days in 2025 when one of his accounts bought a stock while another account sold the same stock the same day. If that is insider trading, it is the worst insider trading in human history, betting for AND against yourself before lunch. That scheme couldn't pour water out of a boot with instructions on the heel.

He does sign the disclosure, though, and he can read his own book after the fact, so it is no blind trust. That is a fair ethics complaint and I'll say it out loud. A computer buying Costco forty times still doesn't show the President traded on secret government information.

Pointing at a Nvidia buy a week before a chip rule and yelling AHA is cum hoc ergo propter hoc, assuming that two things happening at the same time means one caused the other. With 21,000 trades a year, some of them will land next to a headline by pure arithmetic. The broken clock in my classroom is right twice a day and I still had to replace the batteries. I'd grade that logic, Senator, but I don't have a letter below F.

WHO WRITES THE CHECK THE MARKET IS BETTING ON

A stock price is a projection, a guess about how much cash a company will make down the road. For defense contractors, chip makers, drug companies, and solar startups, a huge chunk of that future cash comes from Washington, and Article I, Section 9 says "No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law." Congress writes that law, along with the authorizations, the subsidies, the tax credits, and the multi-year contracts, and committee members see the markup long before the market does. A president can talk a stock up for an afternoon; Congress can hand a company ten years of revenue.

Which brings me to your caucus's favorite stock picker (technically her husband, whose trades she still has to disclose).

o June 2022: Paul Pelosi exercised Nvidia call options worth $1 million to $5 million while the Speaker was moving the CHIPS Act, roughly $53 billion for the semiconductor industry.

o July 26, 2022: he sold 25,000 Nvidia shares, and on July 27 the Senate passed CHIPS. Her office said they don't discuss trades and the sale lost money. Sure, and my students' dogs eat their homework every Tuesday.

o Trackers following the household's disclosures put the strategy around +984% since 2014, against roughly +306% for the S&P 500. That's a tracker estimate and not an audit, but it would make one very lucky man.

o When a ban came up in late 2021, the Speaker said members should be able to participate in the free market.

Jim Quinn's Seventh Law of Liberalism says it's different when you're a Democrat, and here's the proof. A Republican's computer rebalancing an index fund is a constitutional crisis, while a Democrat Speaker's household buying chip options as she pushes a chip bill is "free-market participation." They're muddying the water to make it look deep.

In fairness (and my students will tell you I'm annoyingly fair), your own disclosures show funds and real estate, no individual stocks. Your vote is the problem, Senator, along with Ro Khanna, who sponsors trading bans while his household files trade reports by the thousands. A $174,000 salary does not produce those return curves. My freshmen can do that math, and a few of them still count on their fingers.

WHO ACTUALLY KILLED THE BAN

Trump stood at the State of the Union in February and told Congress to pass the Stop Insider Trading Act without delay. The House passed it in July, 232-198, with 13 House Democrats voting for it, and then your side of the Senate killed it. Jim Quinn's Second Law fits like a glove: if you want to know what liberals are up to, watch what they accuse conservatives of doing.

What's next, Senator? Will you complain that troops went unpaid during a shutdown while every member of Congress got paid on time... wait, I was just told that already happened. A private citizen wrote a $130 million check so our soldiers got paid, and you all collected yours because you wrote the law that way. I broke down the whole racket here, including a real stock ban (no individual stocks for members, spouses, or kids, broad funds or a true blind trust only, and ten times the profit as the penalty): https://t.co/a8kaUTn5th

If you think that's a one-off, take a tour of the worst restaurant in America: https://t.co/Odm2GCHjkB

Congress found $53 billion for chip makers, yet the Major Richard Star Act, about $10 billion over ten years so combat-wounded, medically retired veterans stop having their retirement eaten by an offset, still can't get a floor vote after five Congresses of cosponsors saying nice things and doing nothing for 50,000-plus wounded veterans. I wrote that one for my daughter: https://t.co/tnaDRLFIYZ

So what have you actually done for the people this year, Senator, besides vote no and press record? Most of your bills hand out somebody else's money, and handouts build a dependent voting bloc that has to keep re-electing you to keep the checks coming. You are a snollygoster, which is a shrewd, unprincipled politician (look it up).

And since we're on rich people, I keep hearing millionaire senators say "tax the rich" while knowing every loophole, because their colleagues wrote them. Pay DOUBLE what the IRS says you owe this year, standard deduction only, no itemizing, and then come lecture me about the rich. Until then you're about as useful as a box of white crayons. text:
🇨🇦🇺🇸 What would a political path back to pre-2025 tariff treatment actually look like?

My view: a negotiated package Trump can sell as strengthening North American industry and Carney can sell as restoring reliable trade while protecting Canadian sovereignty.

That means broadly tariff-free trade for qualifying goods again, with longstanding disputes like softwood lumber addressed separately.

Here’s what a possible bargain could look like. 👇

🤝 Start with a reciprocal ceasefire: no new tariffs, import bans or retaliation while negotiations proceed on a defined schedule. Remove existing measures in matched stages, with Canadian concessions tied to American relief actually taking effect.

🏭 On Chinese steel and transshipment, Canada could offer stronger origin verification, customs cooperation and enforcement against proven circumvention. Washington would need to apply equivalent standards at its own ports and remove tariffs on verified Canadian steel and aluminum.

If the concern is unfair Chinese trade, address it together and apply the rules evenly.

🚗 On autos, strengthen enforcement of North American content rules while restoring predictable access for qualifying vehicles and parts. The essential American concession would be accepting that Canadian production contributes to continental competitiveness.

A negotiation becomes much harder if Washington’s definition of success requires Canadian factories moving south.

🥛 On dairy, explore practical improvements to how existing import quotas are administered and used. That could give American exporters something tangible without dismantling supply management. In return, Washington removes the associated punitive measures and uses agreed dispute procedures.

Offering an administrative compromise would not mean conceding that every American allegation is valid.

🥃 On alcohol and procurement, bring the premiers into the negotiation. Provincial restrictions cannot simply be traded away by Ottawa. Their removal should be coordinated with reciprocal American relief and any agreed improvements in market access.

⚡ On energy and critical minerals, offer commercially sound supply agreements, joint investment and faster development of mutually beneficial projects. Canada receives dependable access and opportunities for Canadian businesses in return.

🍁 On sovereignty, Canada could agree to targeted safeguards against trade circumvention while retaining the ability to pursue other trade relationships and protect Canadian culture. Cooperation cannot become a blanket American veto over Canadian decisions.

📜 Then make the settlement durable: extend CUSMA, publish the legal instruments removing tariffs, establish implementation dates and strengthen consultation and dispute resolution. Secure congressional backing where possible.

Another friendly meeting or promise that a deal is “close” will not give businesses the certainty to invest.

🗳️ The political opening also has to come from inside the United States: manufacturers paying more for inputs, farmers losing customers, border communities, governors and members of Congress. Their incentive is protecting American jobs and lowering costs.

The midterms might change that pressure. They will not automatically remove tariffs.

Trump could claim stronger enforcement and improved exporter access. Carney could claim restored trade, protected sovereignty and a future for Canadian manufacturing.

Neither side gets everything. But both countries could recover something worth far more than another victory speech: a dependable trading relationship.

👷 Workers and businesses on both sides need an agreement that lets them build, hire and invest. That is what success should look like.

“Putin’s nuclear threats no longer work,” writes Gideon Rachman in the Financial Times.

Russia possesses the world’s largest nuclear arsenal and constantly reminds the West of it. Moscow has again warned NATO that it is prepared to use “all forces and means at its disposal, including nuclear weapons,” supposedly to defend Russian territory.

On October 1, Vladimir Putin specifically threatened that any attack on Kaliningrad could be met with “all the weapons” Russia possesses. He acknowledged that Britain and France are nuclear powers, but boasted that Russia has no equal in weaponry.

There was a time when such statements dominated headlines. Today, they increasingly pass almost unnoticed.

Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Putin has repeatedly tried to use Russia’s nuclear arsenal to intimidate the West. At first, it worked. The US and its allies were extremely cautious about supplying Ukraine with advanced weapons, partly because of fears that the war could escalate into a nuclear confrontation.

But over time, it became clear that the taboo against nuclear use remains extraordinarily strong.

China and India reportedly warned Moscow against using nuclear weapons. Washington is also believed to have warned Russia of severe consequences, including possible direct Western intervention, if Moscow crossed the nuclear threshold in Ukraine.

As Russian nuclear intimidation lost credibility, Western restrictions gradually weakened. Tanks, fighter aircraft and long-range missiles capable of striking targets inside Russia — once considered too escalatory — eventually reached Ukraine.

In 2025, Ukraine also carried out Operation Spiderweb, a major drone attack against Russia’s strategic bomber fleet. Under Moscow’s own declared doctrine, an attack threatening elements of its nuclear forces could theoretically justify a nuclear response.

Russia did not launch one.

Former NATO Deputy Secretary General Rose Gottemoeller has argued that this demonstrates an uncomfortable reality: nuclear deterrence does not always prevent conventional attacks.

Russia is not the only example. Iran has launched missiles and drones at nuclear-armed Israel. India and Pakistan have exchanged military strikes despite both possessing nuclear weapons.

For Moscow, however, the weakening of nuclear deterrence is particularly painful. Russia’s enormous nuclear arsenal is one of the last foundations of its claim to superpower status — and maintaining it costs an extraordinary amount of money.

Russian commentators still fantasize publicly about nuclear strikes on Europe. But increasingly, Europe simply shrugs.

That is mostly good news.

But it also creates new dangers.

First, Moscow may search for other ways to restore deterrence. Sabotage, assassinations, cyberattacks, drone incursions and other forms of hybrid warfare offer the Kremlin non-nuclear methods of intimidating European supporters of Ukraine.

Second, if nuclear deterrence is becoming less credible, conventional wars may become more likely.

Most European NATO members rely on the US nuclear umbrella. So do Japan and South Korea. If potential adversaries conclude that Washington would never actually risk nuclear war to defend its allies, they may become more willing to test those alliances through conventional military force.

Russia itself could reach the same conclusion regarding NATO.

And finally, everyone is learning nuclear strategy in real time.

The war in Ukraine has forced both Russia and NATO to reconsider assumptions that shaped deterrence for decades. The taboo against nuclear weapons is clearly powerful.

But is it absolute?

Nobody knows.

And that uncertainty may be the most dangerous lesson of all.

Farai, your first principle is correct - diplomacy must serve domestic economic interest. Where you collapse is the maths.

*Let's use real 2024-2026 numbers, not slogans:*

*1. YES, the West is life support for VALUE-ADDED jobs. You are right on this.*
- EU is SA's biggest trading bloc: *€46 billion (R880bn) total trade in 2025*, 23% of all SA trade in goods, 43% of all FDI in SA. 1,700 EU companies employ 500,000 direct jobs + 1.6m indirect. [EU Commission 2025]
- AGOA: *R68bn in 2024 alone*, R300bn between 2019-2024, 22% of all SA exports to US use AGOA. SA is 54% of ALL AGOA exports since 2000. About 500,000 jobs linked. Automotive 22% of SA exports to US ($1.88bn). Citrus, wine, steel. [DTIC / Solidarity]
- When Trump put 30% tariffs in Aug 2025, NAAMSA said it would kill the Eastern Cape auto industry. That is not ideology, that's factories. 718381b3

So if we lose AGOA eligibility in November 2026 review, it's 70,000 direct + 430,000 indirect jobs gone. No one serious denies this.

*2. BUT your "Russia and China will not buy our cars and citrus" - China ALREADY buys more than the US.*

- *China is SA's largest SINGLE export destination:* $13.5bn in 2025 vs US ∼$10bn.
- In June 2026 alone: China ZAR24.1bn, US ZAR14.6bn, Germany ZAR14.1bn exports. [OEC]
- China + India + Thailand + Saudi + UAE = 49.5% of SA imports. Asia has already overtaken Europe as leading import source.[TradeInt] 0f229b05

The problem is STRUCTURAL: We export ores to China (iron, chrome, manganese - 2/3 of exports) and import finished goods (machinery, phones, EVs at HS 8517). We export cars and fruit to EU/US and import machines. That is the colonial division of labour you want to preserve.

China just offered *duty-free access for all African nations* in 2025 - precisely to replace AGOA if US leaves. That's not grandstanding, that's hedging.

*3. BRICS is not about replacing the West, it's about not being held hostage by one market.*

Lamola's real failure is NOT pro-BRICS. It is failing to convert BRICS into beneficiation.

The smart policy is: Keep AGOA + EU EPA (98% duty-free under SADC EPA) for high-value jobs, while using BRICS CTIP deal signed Nov 2025 to force China to buy finished goods, not raw ores. EU signed its own Clean Trade Partnership with SA for the same reason - to secure critical minerals.

Ramaphosa's hedging is not indecision - it is the classic middle-power strategy: Don't pick a side when you are a debtor nation. Indonesia, India, Brazil all do it. Non-alignment pays. The moment you pick Washington fully, you lose Beijing's R200bn import market. Pick Beijing fully, you lose 500k AGOA jobs.

Your critique of Transnet and ports is correct - that's the real reason we have no leverage. Not ICJ. We can have the best diplomats, but if rail can't move cars to Durban, EU and China both go elsewhere.

So the market verdict is not "West vs BRICS". The market verdict is:

- If we lose AGOA in Nov 2026 because of ICJ posturing without a backup plan, that's economic illiteracy.
- If we lose China because we want to please Washington for 4% of total exports (AGOA is <4% of SA total exports), that's also economic illiteracy.

Farai, you are warning about ideological vanity on the left. I am warning about ideological vanity on the right - thinking the West will save us out of goodwill. The West will cut us the same second we are not useful - as they did with 30% tariffs.

Realpolitik = Keep EU + Keep AGOA + Force China to buy beneficiated goods. Not one or the other.

text:
The proposed 2027 Seattle budget would fund 1,250 sworn positions in the Seattle Police Department, 66 more than the current budget. That is a meaningful acknowledgment of a staffing problem that has dogged the city for years.

But there is a problem. At almost the same time Seattle is budgeting for more officers, it is pulling back on some of the tools it has been using to recruit them.

Beginning Sept. 1, SPD stopped offering hiring incentives that included bonuses for new recruits and as much as $50,000 for experienced officers transferring from other departments. SPD said the decision was driven by budget constraints.

The decision to end the bonuses was made by SPD rather than Wilson’s office. But Wilson’s new budget continues the same general shift. According to the Seattle Times, her proposal saves approximately $9.5 million in the police budget by scaling back recruitment and marketing efforts even as it adds funding for those 66 additional sworn positions.

That creates an obvious practical question: if Seattle believes it needs substantially more officers, why reduce the tools designed to attract them before those additional positions are actually filled?

Seattle now has an estimated population of roughly 823,000, but SPD reported just 927 deployable officers in August, or about 1.13 officers per 1,000 residents. That is a significant decline from 2012, when Seattle had about 1,235 deployable officers serving a population of roughly 600,000, or about 2 officers per 1,000 residents. Even under Mayor Wilson’s proposed budget, which would cap the department at 1,151 fully trained officers, Seattle would have only about 1.4 officers per 1,000 residents. Seattle City Councilmember Bob Kettle highlighted the comparison in his review of the mayor’s proposed budget.

Seattle does have an argument for shifting resources away from recruiting. Wilson says more than 3,000 applicants are now in the pipeline and that training, rather than attracting applicants, has become the limiting factor. If that assessment is correct, spending more money on bonuses and advertising may produce diminishing returns.

But this is where two critical realities are being overlooked. First, the number of applicants is not the right metric. The real question is how many of those 3,000 are actually high‑quality candidates – well‑trained, capable, and worthy of wearing the SPD uniform. In perhaps an unintended insight into how Mayor Wilson views law enforcement, policing is much more than “bodies on the street.” It is a profession that demands judgment, training, and character. A large applicant pool is meaningless if only a small fraction meets the standards required to rebuild a depleted department.

Second, one of the most important factors in both recruiting and retention is trust: will the mayor have an officer’s back when it counts? Based on Mayor Wilson’s past comments in support of defunding the police and her hasty dismissal of Chief Barnes, many officers and potential recruits may conclude that the answer is no. That perception directly affects who applies, who stays, and who laterals in. Incentives matter – but leadership confidence matters more.

For a different approach, Seattle only has to look across Lake Washington.

In Bellevue, public safety is viewed as a shared responsibility – and a shared success. The City Council stands squarely behind the Bellevue Police Department, whose officers continue to earn the trust of their community. In fact, Bellevue residents consistently give BPD some of the highest marks in the region, with satisfaction ratings above 90% in annual city surveys.

But Bellevue PD isn’t just recruiting more officers – it’s recruiting officers who can uphold the department’s long‑standing CALEA accreditation. Bellevue has maintained accreditation from the Commission on Accreditation for Law Enforcement Agencies (CALEA) since 2005, a distinction earned by fewer than 6% of law enforcement agencies nationwide. CALEA accreditation is widely recognized as the gold standard in policing, reflecting rigorous training, accountability, and professional excellence.

Bellevue continues to actively compete for experienced officers. The city currently advertises signing bonuses of up to $30,000 for lateral officers and up to $10,000 for certain officers who already have academy certification. It also offers relocation assistance for qualifying candidates, take-home vehicles, and other recruitment and retention benefits.

Those incentives have accompanied tangible hiring gains. Bellevue began 2024 with 32 police vacancies but recruited 46 officers over the following year, producing a net gain of 17 positions. Police Chief Wendell Shirley specifically credited the department’s recruitment package and retention programs, including lateral signing bonuses, take-home vehicles, and wellness benefits.

That is especially notable because Bellevue is becoming an increasingly important competitor to Seattle for more than police officers.

During the first half of 2026, downtown Bellevue leased office space equal to about 6% of its total inventory, compared with about 2% in downtown Seattle. OpenAI, Uber, and Databricks were among the companies making major Bellevue commitments, while commercial real estate researchers described Bellevue as one of the region’s strongest office markets relative to its size.

Public safety is hardly the only factor businesses consider when choosing where to locate, and Bellevue faces its own challenges. But when companies, workers, and families have choices within the same region, the comparison between the two cities is worth watching.

Wilson’s budget acknowledges that Seattle needs more police officers. But adding positions on paper is only the first step. The real test is whether the city is willing to put the resources behind recruiting, training, and retaining enough officers to actually fill them.

Now Seattle residents have an opportunity to weigh in on whether police staffing and public safety receive that priority.

The City Council is currently reviewing Wilson’s proposed 2027–2028 budget, and the coming weeks include several opportunities for public comment. These hearings are an important part of the budget process: Councilmembers can still propose changes before the final budget is adopted. 

The first major public hearing is Tuesday, October 6.

> Remote public testimony begins at 1 p.m., giving residents an opportunity to speak directly to the Council without going to City Hall. Registration for remote testimony opens one hour before the hearing through the Council’s public comment page. Sign up for remote public comment here> https://t.co/UvUTb8f4Nc

> For those who want to testify in person, public comment begins at 5 p.m. at Seattle City Hall, Council Chambers, 600 Fourth Avenue, Seattle, WA 98104. In-person speakers should sign up inside Council Chambers at least 15 minutes before the hearing.

> Residents who cannot testify can also follow the hearing live through the Seattle Channel>https://t.co/YygFDXAriN

Seattle’s budget is ultimately a statement of priorities. If police staffing, recruitment, response times, and public safety are priorities for you, this is an opportunity to make sure Councilmembers hear that directly as they decide where the city’s money goes.

There will be another budget public hearing on November 5, along with additional public-comment opportunities throughout October and November. But Tuesday’s hearing is one of the first major opportunities for residents to weigh in while Councilmembers still have time to reshape the proposal.

text:
Horn Lore📯#13 My beginning. 

I was talking to one of my very closest friends today who asked me why I chose the French Horn. It’s a good question. 

I was about three, maybe four years ago when I started telling everyone I was going only the French horn someday. 

How does a young child even know what a French horn is you ask?  Disney’s “Peter and the Wolf” of course!

A Russian composer named Sergei Prokofiev wrote a story and accompanying music to introduce children to instruments of the orchestra. 

•Peter: The String Family
•Bird: Flute
•Duck: Oboe
•Cat: Clarinet
•Grandfather: Bassoon
•Hunters: Timpani (kettle drums) and bass drum
•Wolf: Three French horns

The sound of that dark horn trio representing the wolf immediately captivated me, and still does. I apparently decided then that I was going to play the horn. 

I entered the 6th grade. We got to choose instruments, so I immediately chose the horn. To my dismay, I was told the horn was much too difficult to start on unless I had a private teacher. I had to choose another. I tried trombone and trumpet, but my heart was broken. 

My amazing parents went on a search and found a horn teacher less than a mile away who was interested in sell his old horn as well as teaching. They jumped on the chance and I got my first horn. It was a simple single horn and I started going to lessons every week. 

As mentioned in earlier posts, there is an extremely steep learning curve for the horn. It can be very frustrating as a young horn player to see others learning their instruments so much quicker. 

I’ll be eternally grateful to my band director. He recognized my hunger to learn and work ethic, so he began choosing repertoire based on the horn part. I was very kid and didn’t like to stand out. I HATED making mistakes and would get very embarrassed when I did. I would therefore play very quietly. My director saw potential in me and began pushing me more and more out of my comfort zone. 

I began to gain courage and drastically improved. Then came my 8th grade year. My director decided to really push me hard and arranged for me play with the high school band for a competition. I was this little shy kid who showed up to much older player and I found I was equal to them. 

I entered high school and met another horn player and we quickly became friends. He was very talented and we started a very friendly rivalry. I won first chair our freshman year. He worked hard and he got first chair our sophomore and junior years. (We traded back and forth though out, but that was what was most of the time). The our senior year, I won first chair and kept it. 

Throughout high school, I was a bit of a science nerd and assumed that’s what I’d pursue as a career. Then came a state-wide band competition. My band was among the best in the state (I was very blessed to be in that school) and we selected some very challenging music. One of the songs we performed featured a very significant horn solo. I don’t now remember what song we played, but I remember knocking the solo out of the park. 

At the end of the performance, the director had me stand first and for the first time in my life a huge auditorium full of people applauded and cheered me on. It was quite overwhelming to me.  

I knew then that music is what I wanted to pursue. I wanted the feeling again. At that competition were several college directors, one of which told me he wanted me to send him an audition tape and practically offered me a scholarship. I eagerly agreed.

My family knew I was pretty good, but had no idea I was that good. I sent in my tape and I was accepted into the UNLV music program as a French horn performance major with a full scholarship. I auditioned and made it into the upper-class band my freshman year. 

After getting married I decided being a professional musician is not the most stable of lifestyles. So I turned the horn into a passionate hobby.

text:
"DeFi is DeFi" is a slogan, not an argument. The question isn't whether the contracts are on-chain -- it's who controls them.

Their own terms name Kayen Labs Inc. 
Inc. means incorporated. Incorporated where? I've searched. No filing, no address, no directors in any registry -- not Delaware, not BVI, not Singapore, not Malta. A name in a ToS is not a legal entity.

And the pause button kills the pure DeFi framing. They confirmed they retain emergency authority to halt the protocol and block withdrawals. 

That's an operator, not a protocol.

MiCA's transition ended 1st July. Serving EU users without a CASP license is now illegal. If they're licensed, show the register entry. If not, 
"DeFi is DeFi" doesn't make it legal.

Here's the killer line: their own terms contain a binding arbitration clause and a class action waiver -- but you can't arbitrate with a company that doesn't exist. Where would the seat be? Which rules? Against whom?

It's not DeFi. It's opaqueness by design. The moment you can administer funds, the moment you can pause funds, it's not just a front-end protocol. It just isn't.

And why even have terms and conditions? They're completely meaningless -- written for an entity that isn't registered anywhere.

Good luck to them in court with "DeFi is DeFi" as a defence. They don't even have a contact page, for gods sake.

And here's the kicker : Chiliz itself warned users on 31st May 2025 -- "We NEVER offer support through Discord, Telegram, or DMs. Beware of scammers." 
Their only official channel is email. 

Yet the only way to reach Kayen is Telegram and Discord. The ecosystem's own parent company flagged exactly this pattern as a scam vector -- and the project they promote runs on it.

But let each one take heed how he builds on it. 11 For no other foundation can anyone lay than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. 12 Now if anyone builds on this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, 13 each one’s work will become clear; for the Day will declare it, because it will be revealed by fire; and the fire will test each one’s work, of what sort it is. 14 If anyone’s work which he has built on it endures, he will receive a reward. 15 If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.1 Corinthians 3:9-15

It’s interesting that Paul opens this letter with the following in 1:4-9

“I thank my God always concerning you for the grace of God which was given to you by Christ Jesus, 5 that you were enriched in everything by Him in all [b]utterance and all knowledge, 6 even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed [c]in you, 7 so that you come short in no gift, eagerly waiting for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ, 8 who will also confirm you to the end, that you may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9 God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of His Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.” 1 Corinthians 1:4-9

Paul says: …
1. that they were enriched in everything by Him…
2. in all [utterance and all knowledge…
3. …even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed [c]in them,
4. …you COME SHORT IN NO GIFT, eagerly waiting for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ…

What makes that so interesting to me is that in the two following verses 10-11 Paul writes:
”…Now I plead with you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment. 11 For it has been declared to me concerning you, my brethren, by those of Chloe’s household, THAT THERE ARE CONTENTIONS AMONG YOU…”

So, here we have the same brethren that “were enriched in everything by Him,” had “all utterance and all knowledge,” “the testimony of Christ was confirmed” in them, and “did not COME SHORT IN NO GIFT”; there were “contentions among” them.

It doesn’t stop there because in 3:1-4 Paul writes:

“And I, brethren, could not speak to you as to spiritual people but as to CARNAL, as to BABES IN CHRIST. 2 I fed you with milk and not with solid food; for until now YOU WERE NOT ABLE TO RECEIVE IT, AND EVEN NOW YOU ARE STILL NOT ABLE; 3 for you are STILL CARNAL. For where THERE ARE ENVY, STRIFE, AND DIVISIONS AMONG YOU, are you not CARNAL AND [A]BEHAVING LIKE MERE MEN? 4 For when one says, “I am of Paul,” and another, “I am of Apollos,” are you not carnal? This leads to what he writes in 3:9-15

If you look closely at the words Paul chose, you learn much about what it is like to have Jesus Christ as our foundation. Paul says we can build on this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, and straw, and that fire will test it all. Obviously, he begins with two metals that fire can’t destroy and could only make them purer. Followed by “precious stones.” To understand “precious stones” in the context of the passage, I researched the effects that fire has on precious stones under the temperatures reached in a house fire and found that most can withstand the heat of fire, some will suffer some damage, some could be severely damaged, and some, like pearls, will evaporate. But wood, hay, and straw will always burn and be destroyed.

What I find interesting is that Paul ends the passage with:

“If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.” Which means to me that if the foundation of a person truly stands on the foundation “which is laid, which is Jesus Christ” nothing he/she builds, whether good or bad cannot affect the salvation of that person.

But let’s continue. Following the flow of the letter: In 5:1-5

It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and such sexual immorality as is not even named among the Gentiles—that a man has his father’s wife! 2 And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, that he who has done this deed might be taken away from among you. 3 For I indeed, as absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged (as though I were present) him who has so done this deed. 4 In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are gathered together, along with my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, 5 deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.”

Again, and following the flow of the letter, this means to me (and I’m definitely open to correction) that this man, who was sleeping with his father’s wife (definitely building with the worst possible kind of straw) was standing on the foundation “which is laid, which is Jesus Christ”; otherwise, how could “…his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus”? Paul assumes he won’t repent, so delivering “…such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” could only mean that whatever horrible thing this “delivering to Satan” was, it was meant to bring him to repentance.

Paul continues in the following chapters up to chapter 10 to address sexual immorality, how to interact with the brethren, and idolatry.

But then we come to chapter 11, where he gives instructions about the Lord’s Supper. In verses 17-22 he writes:

“Now in giving these instructions I do not praise you, since you come together not for the better but for the worse. 18 For first of all, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it. 19 For there must also be factions among you, that those who are approved may be [b]recognized among you. 20 Therefore WHEN YOU COME TOGETHER IN ONE PLACE, IT IS NOT TO EAT THE LORD’S SUPPER. 21 For in eating, each one takes his own supper ahead of others; and one is hungry and another is drunk. 22 What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and shame [c]those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you in this? I do not praise you.”

These brethren were something else! They would fight about who would eat first; some came not to celebrate the sacred communion but to satisfy their hunger, and to top it off, some would get drunk! Paul continues in verses 27-32

“Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks this cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. 28 But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. 29 For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy manner eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the Lord’s body. 30 For this reason MANY ARE WEAK and SICK among you, and MANY [I]SLEEP. 31 For if we would judge ourselves, we would not be judged. 32 But when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with the world.”

Again, these crazy brethren conducting themselves in such an evil and despicable manner (building with straw) during the sacred celebration of the Lord’s Supper had to obviously be standing on the foundation “which is laid, which is Jesus Christ”; otherwise Jesus would not have made “some sick and weak,” and some put them to sleep (take home early) if they weren’t standing on the foundation “which is laid, which is Jesus Christ” and if they didn’t belong to Him.

So, two things that I must say. First, if you, who read this, at one time walked with God and were close to Him, but for different reasons have lost your way, if (IF!) you, in your disobedient lifestyle, long for God’s presence and to be right with Him again, you are still saved. That is the Holy Spirit that would not call you and draw you otherwise. But you must also be aware of the consequences your evil ways have brought upon you and possibly those you love. On the other hand, if you have no desire to be right with God and feel that you are saved, and because you are saved you can’t lose your salvation and could engage in evil and sinful behavior, you are not saved! He “never knew you!”

Secondly, I’m grieved by how many, a dime a dozen (heresy hunters), question people’s salvation because of something they believe or don’t believe, and accuse people of being “heretics”, “false teachers”, and “false prophets”, and hurt the conscience of so many young believers who had a real born-again experience when coming to Christ.

I strongly challenge the notion that “correct doctrine” is necessary for salvation. I strongly believe that Romans 10:5-13

For Moses writes about the righteousness which is of the law, “The man who does those things shall live by them.” 6 But the righteousness of faith speaks in this way, “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’ ” (that is, to bring Christ down from above) 7 or, “ ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’ ” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). 8 But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith which we preach): 9 that if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God has raised Him from the dead, you will be saved. 10 For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. 11 For the Scripture says, “Whoever believes on Him will not be put to shame.” 12 For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord over all is rich to all who call upon Him. 13 For “whoever calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved.”

Is all one needs to be saved. I also strongly believe that anyone who is truly saved knows it. A witness in their heart comes from true salvation. But let me explain a bit further. Let’s assume someone in a remote village isolated from modern-day technology in a South American country hears the gospel, believes it, is given a Bible in their language, and begins to read on their own. Obviously, they are going to interpret, or we could also say that God will speak to them through His Word differently than to someone who has lived all his life in a modern Western society. And God will hold them accountable for that truth. In a few words: God is more interested in a hungry heart for Him that truly loves Him and His Word and reads to understand His way, than in correct interpretation of Scripture. Too many, a dime a dozen, question people’s salvation based on a different way of understanding Scripture that does little or nothing to affect the Truth we find in Romans 10:5-13.

What I have shared about what Paul teaches us in 1 Corinthians shows us that salvation is not a fragile, delicate reality that could be shattered or burned away because of our evil ways. Are there consequences, many times severe consequences, when we stand on the Foundation and think it’s a good idea to go crazy living a life of sin? Absolutely! You better believe it! But questioning someone’s salvation because they believe the “prosperity gospel”, or the “exposure gospel” or the catholic, calvanist or any other denomination based on the interpretation of a verse or passage of Scripture that has nothing to do with Romans 10:5-13 is wrong and unnecessary. When people believe false and wrong doctrines, God is concerned first with their heart, and He will lead everyone to the Truth that He wants them to believe. The basic tenets of Scripture are easy for anyone, even a 5-year-old, to understand. Do I not believe that proper interpretation of Scripture is important? Absolutely not! What I am saying is that before correct interpretation of Scripture comes a heart that genuinely wants to know and fellowship with God. In God’s eyes, someone with “correct” interpretation may not be as pleasing, or pleasing at all, to Him as someone with a clean and pure heart who needs to work on his/her interpretation of Scripture.

One last passage of 1 Corinthians, and I’m done. In chapter 10:27-33:

If any of those who do not believe invites you to dinner, and you desire to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no question for conscience’ sake. 28 But if anyone says to you, “This was offered to idols,” do not eat it for the sake of the one who told you, and for conscience’ sake; [i]for “the earth is the Lord’s, and all its fullness.” 29 “Conscience,” I say, not your own, but that of the other. For why is my liberty judged by another man’sconscience? 30 But if I partake with thanks, why am I evil spoken of for the food over which I give thanks? 31 Therefore, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God. 32 Give no offense, either to the Jews or to the Greeks or to the church of God, 33 just as I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of many, that they may be saved.”

In this passage, Paul presents the reader with a very interesting situation. He says that if someone who does "not believe" invites you to dinner and you (a believer) desire to go, you are free to eat anything they put before you. Meaning that even if the food could have very well been “offered to idols” (demons), you are free to eat because you “…partake with thanks; why am I evil spoken of for the food over which I give thanks?” Meaning that you bless the food and partake with thanksgiving, and God takes care of the rest.

But if they tell you that it has been “offered to idols,” then you must abstain, not because knowing makes the food any different, less nutritious or poisonous, but because it will lead them to believe that offering food “offered to idols” (demons) is ok, which obviouly is not.

At the end of the day, salvation cannot be lost. If God saves you, He will keep you saved. If I’m wrong and salvation can be lost, then that’s it. You could never be saved “again”. The Holy Spirit would not draw you. You can only be born again once in a lifetime; there’s no such thing as multiple “born again” experiences for anyone!
