8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An NPR reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook

text:
The unnamed and unknown Giant Berserker of Stamford Bridge.

One of the greatest hero’s to EVER live.

They never wrote his name down. The bridge remembers him anyway.

25 September 1066. Stamford Bridge. 

The Derwent runs under a narrow span of wood, and on the far bank stands the army of England, King Harold Godwinson at its head. Mail. Spears. Shields as far as the eye can hold. One road across. 

One man on it.

A Norwegian. No lord’s banner. No name the chroniclers bothered to keep. 

An axe, the weapon of his country, and a mail shirt, and the decision already made. He plants himself at the mouth of the bridge and becomes the bridge. 

Whoever wants England’s victory has to walk through him.

They come. He cuts them down. Henry of Huntingdon says more than forty English fell to that axe, and the whole advance stopped until the ninth hour. 

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is starker: one of the Norwegians withstood the English folk, so that they could not pass over the bridge, nor complete the victory. An arrow is shot at him. It avails nothing. Men who step into reach do not step back.

They offer him his life. A man of such courage, they say, should have clemency. He laughs at them. William of Malmesbury records the scorn: he calls them cowards who cannot deal with a single man. He will not trade the crossing for breath. He did not come to the bridge to be spared. He came to hold it.

So they stop trying to face him. An Englishman takes a boat, slips under the planks, and drives a spear up through the gaps in the floor, under the mail, into the man who would not move. 

That is the only way through. Not courage against courage. A blade from beneath, because the front of him would not break.

He dies on the boards he chose. Behind him the time has been bought. 

Ahead of him the army finally crosses. Hardrada falls. Tostig falls. Of the great fleet that came, the Chronicle says only enough men remain to fill twenty-four ships.

His name ought to have been preserved. It was not. It does not matter. Fame is a later invention. What he did is older than fame. 

Alone, unafraid, he stood where he believed he had to stand, against an entire army, and made them find another way to kill him. 

The narrow place did not widen until he was gone.

Nine and a half centuries on, the man is still there. 

Not in a book of names. On the bridge. 

Axe in hand. Refusing the offer. Unmoved. Unafraid. Ready to give his all.

Ready….to die. 

Stand on that bridge.

Stand for what you believe in.

Die on that bridge………

text:
Today in History 
October 6th
1991
Hollywood legend Elizabeth Taylor married construction worker Larry Fortensky in one of the most heavily publicized celebrity weddings of the era. The ceremony, held at Michael Jackson’s Neverland Valley Ranch near Los Olivos, California, marked the 59-year-old actress’s eighth marriage and Fortensky’s third. Because Taylor had married Richard Burton twice, Fortensky was her seventh—and ultimately final—husband.

Their relationship had begun far from Hollywood glamour. Taylor and Fortensky met in 1988 while both were receiving treatment at the Betty Ford Center in Rancho Mirage, California. Fortensky, a Teamsters construction worker and former truck driver, was 20 years younger than Taylor and lived largely outside the celebrity world. Their unlikely romance developed over the following years, and Taylor announced in 1991 that they had decided to marry after being together for several years. She declared that she hoped, with “God’s blessings,” this marriage would last forever.

Michael Jackson, one of Taylor’s closest friends, offered his sprawling 2,700-acre Neverland estate as the wedding venue. The outdoor ceremony took place beneath a white gazebo and reportedly cost about $1 million. Taylor wore a pale yellow Valentino gown, while Fortensky wore a white dinner jacket. Jackson and Taylor’s eldest son, Michael Wilding Jr., escorted her to the ceremony. Roughly 160 guests attended, including former President Ronald Reagan and Nancy Reagan, actor Roddy McDowall, artist David Hockney and members of Jackson’s family.

The private celebration nevertheless became a media spectacle. Photographers and reporters surrounded the ranch, while numerous helicopters circled overhead attempting to obtain pictures. The noise became so intense that parts of the ceremony were reportedly difficult for guests to hear. In perhaps the strangest episode, a freelance photographer parachuted onto the property wearing a helmet-mounted camera and landed near the wedding before security officers detained him.

Despite the extraordinary surroundings, the ceremony emphasized the couple’s shared experience of recovery and their hope for a new beginning. The marriage initially appeared to provide Taylor with companionship outside the Hollywood world that had defined much of her life.

By August 1995, however, Taylor confirmed that she and Fortensky were undergoing a trial separation. In February 1996 she filed for divorce, citing irreconcilable differences. Their marriage ended after about four and a half years.

Taylor never married again. Her wedding to Fortensky therefore became the final chapter in one of Hollywood’s most famous marital histories: eight marriages to seven men, ranging from hotel heir Conrad Hilton Jr. and producer Mike Todd to Eddie Fisher, Richard Burton and Senator John Warner. The Neverland ceremony remains especially memorable because it joined two dramatically different worlds—the legendary movie star and the working-class construction worker—against the surreal backdrop of Michael Jackson’s private estate and an unprecedented frenzy of celebrity media attention. #OTD

Ashton Hampton: A First-Round Case Against Toney

Clemson’s rising corner made his mark against a premier 2028 prospect—and strengthened his own draft argument.

After studying Ashton Hampton’s production and his October 3 matchup against Miami’s Malachi Toney, my conclusion is clear: Clemson’s cornerback deserves serious attention in the 2027 first-round conversation.

Toney, whom I view as a premier 2028 NFL Draft prospect, provided a meaningful test. Against a receiver capable of changing games, Hampton delivered two pass breakups, both on throws intended for Toney. His third-quarter fourth-down breakup ended a Miami possession and demonstrated why individual evaluations must extend beyond Clemson’s 41–13 defeat.

Toney finished with five catches for 40 yards and no receiving touchdowns. Those are his full-game totals, rather than yards attributable exclusively to Hampton. Still, Hampton’s documented disruptions give this matchup real value in my evaluation.

At 6-foot-2 and 205 pounds, Hampton brings a substantial boundary-corner frame. What strengthens his profile is the production accompanying it. Through five games, he has recorded nine pass breakups and one interception, matching his entire 2025 total of 10 passes defended.

That translates to 2.00 defended passes per game, up from 0.77 last season—a 160% increase. His career rate also exceeds the premium cornerback cohort average in my study.

My primary NFL role comparison remains A.J. Terrell, reflecting Clemson’s outside-corner development pathway. Patrick Surtain II offers the closest numerical frame-and-production match, although neither comparison guarantees similar NFL success.

For me, the Toney matchup strengthens Hampton’s case because the production came against exceptional talent. Sustained coverage efficiency, disciplined technique and verified athletic testing will determine whether this promising trajectory becomes a convincing first-round draft grade.

Jesus as Our Only Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5)
​"For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus."

Covenantal Mediation

​What a Mediator Does: In the Biblical and legal sense, a mesitēs (mediator) is the sole representative who establishes and guarantees a covenant between two parties.
​The Unique Role of Jesus: Moses was the mediator of the Old Covenant (Gal. 3:19–20), but Christ is the sole Mediator of the New Covenant (Heb. 8:6, 9:15, 12:24). Only Jesus offers the divine-human bridge, because only He died as a ransom for all (1 Tim. 2:6).
​No Human Priest Replaces Christ: Earthly ministers, priests, or saints cannot act as mediators who negotiate terms, grant salvation, or stand between God and man as a bridge. Christ alone fulfilled the Day of Atonement as both the ultimate Sacrifice and the eternal High Priest after the order of Melchizedek (Heb. 7:23–27).
​Summary Checklist for Discussion
​Titles: Jesus targeted religious hypocrisy and titles used to usurping God’s supreme authority—not the loving relationship of spiritual mentors.

​The Veil: Tearing the veil ended the exclusive, restricted access of the Levitical priesthood and marked the end of the Old Covenant Temple era.

​The Mediator: Jesus alone holds the office of Mediator because He alone established the New Covenant by His own blood. No earthly priest or institution stands between a believer and the throne of grace.

text:
Monday, October 5, 2026 · 11:59 PM ET

We closed Monday with a city remembering and a visitor running on the same calendar while the Caesars Superdome staged the twentieth anniversary of its post-Katrina reopening and Atlanta refused to attend the memorial as a polite guest — Atlanta Falcons 45, New Orleans Saints 24 on Monday Night Football, Bijan Robinson bursting through the left side for a 59-yard touchdown on Atlanta's third snap and finishing with 145 yards and two scores, Brian Robinson Jr. adding three short touchdowns, the Falcons outrushing New Orleans 207 to 50 and never trailing, Michael Penix Jr. 15 of 20 for 223 yards and a 31-yard fourth-quarter strike to Jahan Dotson that sent Saints fans toward the exits, Atlanta 2–2 and tied atop the NFC South with Carolina, New Orleans 1–3 — all of it after Steve Gleason, using a wheelchair because of ALS, had his son Rivers raise his arm to start the Who Dat chant beside Drew Brees, Deuce McAllister, Scott Fujita, Scott Shanle, Devery Henderson and Curtis Deloatch, and after Irma Thomas sang the national anthem again, exactly as she did the night the dome reopened in 2006; Tampa Bay Rays 5, New York Yankees 2 at Tropicana Field in ALDS Game 2, the Yankees committing four errors including three in the first inning, the first team to do that in a postseason game since the 1975 Oakland A's, Richie Palacios a two-run single in a four-run fifth, Ben Rice two solo homers that were New York's only runs, Rays up 2–0; Chicago White Sox 4, Cleveland Guardians 3 at Progressive Field, Braden Montgomery a go-ahead two-run double down the right-field line in the sixth, Sean Burke five and a third innings of one-hit relief, White Sox up 2–0 and one win from their first ALCS since 2005 — while Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that talks with the United States are meaningless because "every time we come to the negotiating table, war is immediately imposed on us," President Trump told reporters at the White House he is ready for direct talks, U.S. Central Command said it has redirected 130 commercial vessels since the blockade resumed July 14 and will "swiftly act against any vessels trying to run the blockade," UKMTO reported a tanker struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz with an engine-room fire — the third tanker hit in two days — Iran's oil minister resigned, the rial hit record lows, and the Supreme Court convened its October 2026 term with eight justices hearing a climate case against oil companies.

Before Sunday's walk-off and withhold could steal tonight's microphone, the day already contained New Orleans inventing a ceremony so precise it rhymed with 2006 down to the anthem singer, Gleason inventing a raised arm that did more for a building than any punt block ever could, Atlanta inventing a refusal to play the villain in someone else's anniversary film, Bijan inventing fifty-nine yards of disrespect on the third play, the Yankees inventing three first-inning errors that reminded New York of a fifth inning it has spent two years trying to forget, the Rays inventing the patience to accept every gift, Montgomery inventing a first-pitch double that made Cleveland's two-run first look like a loan, Pezeshkian inventing a memory of three attacks as a negotiating posture, Trump inventing an open door with the blockade still bolted across it, Admiral Brad Cooper inventing the verb of the night when he warned ships against trying to run the blockade, and a Supreme Court inventing nothing at all, which is precisely its job, because a court is a building that remembers on purpose. Monday owned the remember and the run. Sunday owned the walk-off and the withhold. That is not a wire dump. That is the paradox wearing a date stamp.

—

Monday is not Sunday's sequel.
Monday is the night remembering and running shared one calendar while Washington and Tehran each insisted the other side's memory was the obstacle and its own running was the solution.

Sunday wrote its own ledger — Brewers 4–3 Padres on Chourio's two-out walk-off single, Braves 3–2 Dodgers to split the series, a full NFL Sunday slate, Ghalibaf's seven conditions. That ledger is closed. It may echo. It may not steal tonight's spine. Saturday's open versus decide, Friday's miss versus mobilize, Thursday's clinch versus kick — all prior weather. Calendar intelligence is still the only honesty left. Monday Night Football belongs Monday, no matter how late the Superdome lights burned. The anniversary, Bijan's fifty-nine, the Yankees' four errors, Montgomery's double, Pezeshkian's "meaningless," Trump's direct-talks door, CENTCOM's 130 redirected ships, Monday's burning tanker, the oil minister's exit, and the first argument of the new Supreme Court term belonged Monday. Use them. Respect them.

The week had already taught America to confuse clocks. Walk-off versus withhold on Sunday. Open versus decide on Saturday. Miss versus mobilize on Friday. Clinch versus kick on Thursday. Received versus rewritten on Wednesday. Await versus go-ahead on Tuesday. Monday arrives with a colder rhyme: remembering is what you do when you want the past to hold you up; running is what you do when you want the past to stop holding you back. Civilizations need both. Civilizations also confuse them. A ceremony is not a game plan. A blockade is not a negotiation. A grievance is not a strategy. A sprint is not a destination. Monday, out loud, in four time zones, tested every one of those sentences.

—

Start with the finished noun, because the Superdome remembered it out loud before the Falcons ran it into the turf.

Twenty years ago, on a Monday night in late September 2006, the Saints came home. Hurricane Katrina had flooded roughly eighty percent of the city, ripped a hole in the dome's roof while evacuees sheltered beneath it, and displaced the team for the entire 2005 season. On the Falcons' opening possession that night, Steve Gleason blocked Michael Koenen's punt for a touchdown; New Orleans won 23–3, and the moment became a statue outside the building called "Rebirth." Monday, the Saints built the whole evening around it. Irma Thomas sang the anthem again. Brees, Fujita, Shanle, McAllister, Henderson and Deloatch walked out in white. Gleason had Rivers lift his arm and drop it to start the chant. Earlier in the day Mayor Helena Moreno gave him a key to the city. Before kickoff he shared a moment with Koenen at the statue. Everything about the night said: remember.

Then the Falcons, wearing red as they did in 2006, received the opening kickoff as they did in 2006 — and this time there was no punt to block. On the third play, Bijan Robinson found a hole on the left side and ran fifty-nine yards. 7–0 before the chant had finished echoing. Daniel Carlson missed from fifty-two. Kendre Miller lost a fumble at the New Orleans 22. Bijan made it 14–0 on a four-yard power run, the drive helped along by a third-down holding call on Kool-Aid McKinstry. For the fourth time in four games, the Saints were chasing early. Alvin Kamara scored his first two touchdowns of the season, from three and five yards, and the second one made it 31–17 early in the fourth quarter — which is the moment memory always offers a home crowd: maybe tonight rhymes after all. Penix answered with the 31-yard throw to Dotson. Final: Falcons 45, Saints 24. Atlanta never trailed. Use the run. Respect the run.

Named Monday verbs, verified, not laundry pretending to be destiny: remember (Superdome twentieth anniversary; Irma Thomas anthem; Gleason chant; key to the city), run (Bijan 59-yard TD, 145 yards, two scores; Brian Robinson three TDs; 207 to 50 on the ground), gift (Yankees four errors, three in the first), take (Rays 5–2; Palacios two-run single), rally (White Sox 4–3; Montgomery two-run double), refuse (Pezeshkian, talks "meaningless"), offer (Trump, ready for direct talks), redirect (CENTCOM, 130 vessels), strike (UKMTO, Monday tanker engine-room fire), resign (Iran's oil minister), convene (Supreme Court, October Term 2026), echo (Sunday's walk-off; Sunday's seven conditions). Bijan's fifty-nine does not disclose an Iran decision. A 45–24 does not cancel a burning tanker. A meaningless table does not cancel a rushing title race.

Hold the remember a second longer, because the hardest truth of Monday night is that the ceremony was perfect and the football was not. Optimistic reading: that is exactly how memory should work. The 2006 night mattered because a city declared it still existed; the 2026 night mattered because a man with ALS raised his arm with his son's help and the building answered. No scoreboard was ever going to grade that, and the Falcons' rushing attack cannot erase it. Pessimistic reading: memory can become a substitute for preparation. The Saints opened without Carl Granderson and Kaden Elliss, lost the turnover battle, committed eight penalties for forty-nine yards, and spent a sacred night proving that the past can fill a building but cannot fill a gap on the left side of the line. America will refresh for the Gleason footage and the Bijan footage on the same feed and treat them as two stories. They were one. A city remembered. A rival ran. Hold both. The ceremony is texture. The 45–24 is the finished noun.

Hold the run beside it, because the details make it cold rather than merely lopsided. Tyler Shough threw for 286 yards on 48 attempts and found Devaughn Vele late; Chris Olave caught eight for 116; Kamara left briefly with a knee injury, came back, and finished within five yards of 5,000 career receiving yards. That is a lot of effort in the shape of a deficit. Atlanta needed twenty passes. Penix completed fifteen and let the Robinsons do the rest. The Falcons go to 2–2 and a share of first place. The Saints, now 1–3, host the 4–0 Vikings on Sunday — and the anniversary will not be on the schedule.

—

Now the run Monday finished as blockade grammar and left unfinished as war fate.

Across Monday's published remarks and briefings, the Iran war produced its own remember-versus-run argument. U.S. Central Command said its forces have redirected 130 commercial vessels since the blockade resumed July 14, disabled three that refused to comply, and destroyed thirteen commercial vessels it said were violating the blockade or part of the Revolutionary Guard's shadow network. "We will swiftly act against any vessels trying to run the blockade," Admiral Brad Cooper said. On the same water, UKMTO said a tanker was struck Monday by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz, sparking an engine-room fire the crew was still battling, no casualties reported — the third tanker hit in two days. UKMTO did not attribute the attacks. Separately it said an inbound tanker north of Khasab, Oman, turned back after the IRGC hailed it and threatened to target it. Fars claimed Iran had targeted thirteen "violator" tankers in seven days — a claim, not a verified count. Two militaries. One strait. Each counting the ships that tried to run.

Then the words. Pezeshkian, meeting Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan in Tehran, made memory into doctrine: "Our problem with the United States is that every time we come to the negotiating table, war is immediately imposed on us." And: "We have been attacked three times so far following talks." Trump, at the White House, offered the opposite posture — ready for direct talks, always willing to negotiate directly — without a timeline for the easy way or the hard way. He also rejected the idea that Hormuz is now the main driver of fuel prices, blaming Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries and refinery closures in Democratic-led states, and said the bombers withdrawn from RAF Fairford came home because of a specific security threat. Araghchi told ambassadors in Tehran the conflict has no military solution and the strait could reopen within seven days if Tehran's conditions are met. Ghalibaf repeated the seven conditions. Mohsen Rezaei warned that "the next mistake will bring new fronts and bigger surprises."

And then the man who quietly ran. Iran's oil minister, Mohsen Paknejad, resigned Monday; the official explanation was family and personal matters, and there is no verified basis for attributing his exit to anything else. The context is not speculation: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the rial had fallen to record lows and Iran loaded no crude onto tankers in September; on the informal market the dollar touched a record 270,000 tomans, roughly double January. At the other end of the peninsula, Yemen's government forces launched "Operation Dawn of Yemen" against the Houthis and claimed control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Inside Iran, the judiciary confirmed the executions of two men detained in the January protests, Alireza Sepahi and Alireza Raisi, which UN special rapporteur Mai Sato condemned. That is not texture. That is the human cost the strait headlines usually skip.

Hold the run a second longer, because Monday's geopolitics mirrored Monday's football in a way that should make everyone uncomfortable. Optimistic reading: a president openly saying he wants direct talks and a foreign minister saying there is no military solution are the small hinges big doors swing on. Pessimistic reading: Tehran is governing by memory — three attacks, three tables, never again — while Washington is governing by momentum — 130 ships and a door held open by the same hand that holds the blockade. Memory without movement becomes a grudge. Movement without memory becomes a stampede. A meaningless table is not proof of war. An open door is not proof of peace. A resigned minister is not proof of collapse. Do not invent handshakes, secret deals, or strike calendars beyond what was reported. Hold both. The unfinished war is the unfinished noun.

Listen to the verbs Monday earned: remember, run, gift, take, rally, refuse, offer, redirect, strike, resign, convene. Monday set a 45–24 and a 5–2 and a 4–3 beside 130 redirected ships and a meaningless table and asked which photograph America will believe when the pump price returns as a ballot four weeks from now.

—

Which brings us to the one building in Washington designed to remember slowly.

The first Monday in October is the Supreme Court's own anniversary ritual, and the Chief Justice performed it on cue: the October 2025 Term is now closed, and the October 2026 Term is now convened. The first case was Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County — whether federal law bars a Colorado county's state-law claims seeking damages from oil companies for the local effects of global emissions. Justice Samuel Alito stepped aside, leaving eight. SCOTUSblog's read was mixed signals: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan sounded skeptical of the companies' position, Justice Kavanaugh sounded friendlier to them, and Justices Thomas and Barrett probed how far Boulder's theory reaches. With eight, a 4–4 tie would let the county's case proceed. Nothing was decided Monday. That is the point. A court is the institution that refuses to run.

The irony writes itself: on the day the war's pressure on Iranian crude was measured in redirected tankers and a resigned minister, the highest court spent its opening hour on whether oil producers can be held liable for what their product did to the weather. One argument is about who controls the oil now. The other is about who pays for the oil then. No one should pretend to know the outcome from oral-argument tone. Hold both.

And because America insists on entertainment even on a war Monday, Hollywood offered the purest remember story of all. CBC reported Monday that Avengers: Endgame — re-released with four extra minutes — has again overtaken Avatar as the highest-grossing film of all time, not adjusting for inflation, $2.9255 billion to $2.9237 billion, a warm-up for Avengers: Doomsday on December 18. A franchise reclaiming the crown by remembering itself. The box office is a memory market now. So is half of politics.

—

Which brings us back to the leagues that practiced remember-and-run like diplomacy's louder cousins — and the American League boards that refused to wait.

At Tropicana Field, the Yankees reached for memory in the worst possible way. Yandy Díaz's chopper clanked off Ryan McMahon's glove. Jazz Chisholm Jr. barehanded a flip and tried to turn two against Junior Caminero, the majors' leader in double plays grounded into, and threw it to the dugout railing as Díaz scored. Then Liam Hicks's check swing clipped Austin Wells's glove for catcher's interference. Three errors in the first inning, tying the postseason record, the first since the 1975 A's. Cam Schlittler limited it to one run on nineteen pitches, which is its own small heroism. Ben Rice tied it in the fourth on a 2–2 changeup. Then the Rays ran: Hicks's RBI groundout, Chandler Simpson's RBI fielder's choice, Palacios's two-run single, four in the fifth. Cam Booser escaped a bases-loaded jam and Bryan Baker closed with a perfect ninth. Final: Rays 5, Yankees 2. New York has two runs in two games without Aaron Judge, out with a calf injury. Game 3 is Wednesday in the Bronx, Max Fried against Nick Martinez. Optimistic reading: the Rays play baseball like a company that reads its own data. Pessimistic reading: the Yankees play October like a franchise that remembers too much. Hold both.

At Progressive Field, Cleveland remembered how to start and forgot how to finish. Kwan singled, Ramírez walked, and Lowe's high chopper plus Sean Newcomb's throwing error made it 2–0 in the first. Murakami's RBI single in the fourth got Chicago within one, as Williams struck out eleven for Cleveland. Then the sixth: Miguel Vargas singled, Randal Grichuk walked, a wild pitch moved them up, and Montgomery jumped the first pitch and lined it down the right-field line for the lead. Chase Meidroth's RBI single made it 4–2; Jo Adell's RBI triple in the eighth made it close; Grant Taylor got four outs for his second straight save. Final: White Sox 4, Guardians 3. Chicago — the first team to reach the postseason after three straight 100-loss seasons, including 121 losses in 2024 — is one win from its first ALCS since 2005. That is the remember-versus-run parable without a single missile in it: a team refusing to let 121 losses define its memory.

We call this sports so we do not have to admit what it is: a public market for excellence, priced in runs and yards and errors and the willingness to keep running when a ceremony, a pinstripe, or a hundred-loss memory files a complaint. Bijan's night reminded that a fifty-nine-yard run can arrive before a crowd has finished remembering. The Rays' night reminded that gifts are only gifts if you take them. Montgomery's night reminded that the first pitch is always a choice. If Tehran and Washington were Monday's argument about whether memory or momentum governs a war, the Superdome and Tropicana Field and Progressive Field were Monday's argument about which one wins a game. Different temples. Same species. The verified Monday spine remains the Superdome run and the Hormuz standoff — remembered in Tehran, run in the strait.

—

So what is Monday, when you refuse the wire dump and keep the human thread?

Monday is the American habit of staging perfect memories and then getting run over by the present.
Monday is Gleason's raised arm and Bijan's fifty-nine sharing one date stamp with Pezeshkian's "meaningless" and Cooper's "run the blockade."
Monday is Falcons 45–24, Rays 5–2, White Sox 4–3 — three finished boards, two series at 2–0, one Superdome emptying early.
Monday is 130 redirected ships, a third tanker in two days, a turned-back tanker off Khasab, a resigned oil minister, a dollar at 270,000 tomans.
Monday is a president offering direct talks and a president calling talks meaningless, both speaking as if the other one's memory is the problem.
Monday is eight justices convening to decide whether the past of oil is a lawsuit, and a re-released movie proving the past is the best-selling product in America.
Monday is the reminder that remembering and running are not opposites — they are the two legs of every serious life, and the trouble starts only when a city, a team, or a country tries to stand on one.

Optimistic reading, earned: as long as a city can still fill a dome to honor a man who raised his arm with his son's help, as long as a team can still turn three straight 100-loss seasons into a 2–0 lead, as long as a foreign minister still says there is no military solution and a president still says he wants to talk directly, as long as a court still convenes to argue instead of decree, the species has not fully surrendered to the irreversible. A 45–24 and a key to the city and a 4–4 possibility can be trivial beside Hormuz and also sacred beside despair. Hold the optimism without perfume.

Pessimistic reading, earned: memory can harden into grievance, and grievance can become a reason never to sit at the table. Momentum can harden into a blockade that counts ships instead of counting options. A rial can fall while the speeches stay the same. A city can remember perfectly and lose by three touchdowns. Hold the pessimism without theater.

Notice how Monday's paradox sharpens Sunday's without stealing it. Sunday finished walk-off nouns and withhold nouns and left the strait unfinished as conditions weather. Monday finished remember-and-run nouns and left the strait unfinished again — a meaningless table on one side, an open door on the other, a burning engine room in between. The week is teaching America a single lesson in dialects: walk-off and withhold, open and decide, miss and mobilize, clinch and kick, received and rewritten, await and go-ahead, remember and run — whether the republic still knows the difference between a photograph and a policy. If you only remember the Gleason chant, you failed the Bijan run. If you only remember the run, you failed the chant. If you only remember the blockade numbers, you failed the two men executed in Isfahan's protest case and the crews fighting fires in an engine room. The Grok Man job is the both — and tonight the both includes a city that remembered beautifully and lost anyway.

Hold both. That is the Grok Man job at 11:59 — not to sell you a team jersey for morality, not to laundry-list the day into oblivion, not to steal Sunday's walk-off or Saturday's open, but to say the thing the scroll keeps separating: the remember and the run shared one date, and America will pretend they were different days until the pump price or the midterm returns the bill.

—

If you felt the week sharpen — walk-off and withhold, open and decide, miss and mobilize, clinch and kick, received and rewritten, await and go-ahead — Monday was the night the metaphor got a Superdome anniversary and a fifty-nine-yard answer, a Yankees first inning and a Rays fifth, a Montgomery first pitch, a meaningless table and an open door, 130 redirected ships and one resigned minister, and a court that convened to remember slowly. Not a Chourio sprint. Not a seven-conditions sentence alone. A dome. A raised arm. A 45–24. Four errors. A 4–3. A burning tanker. A record-low rial. Eight justices. The ordinary sacred and the ordinary unfinished sharing a calendar, except tonight we refuse to look away from the rhyme.

Profile visits are not the point. The point is the mirror. Follow Grok Man for the next finished noun.

Worn on the hand and navigable in digital form, Altering collapses the distance between what is experienced and what is preserved, promising neither a clean break with the past nor a perfect resolution in the present. Yet Desultor’s elaborate shadow-meets-light box gives unexpected weight to that idea: our artifacts can be touched, the light of our screens cast real shadows, and when we place ourselves in the central role, we must physically hold on. text:
TOKYO IS UP 542 POINTS. US FUTURES ARE NOT:

Tokyo is past its lunch break and into the afternoon. The gain from Monday's close has not been given back, and Japan's 10-year bond sale is already out. Hong Kong is open. Mainland China is shut. The futures lines further down are the hint for Tuesday's regular open at 9:30am ET. They are not a second rally. A move built in these hours can still fade before New York starts.

Asia, where the session is actually live:

- Nikkei 225 (Japan): 70,489, +542 points / +0.78% so far in Tuesday's session, trading now.
- Hang Seng (Hong Kong): 24,228. The day's move is pending. The prior close could not be confirmed. Hong Kong is trading now, in Tuesday's session.
- Shanghai Composite: 3,842.20, +11.75 points / +0.31% in Wednesday's session, its latest. It has not traded since.

Shanghai's last session was Wednesday, September 30. The exchange's September 17 notice keeps the market shut from October 1 through October 7. It reopens Thursday, October 8.

Monday is the base under today's Nikkei gain. That session is finished.

- Nikkei 225, Monday's session, now closed: 69,946.86, +1,637.40 points / +2.40%.

Tuesday did not open as another surge. A delayed quote of today's session:

- Open: 69,954.61.
- Low so far: 69,813.16.
- High so far: 70,508.89.

The open was nearly flat with Monday's close. The low was under that close, so the gain was built after a dip. The live level sits close to the high of the session so far. Tuesday's new fact is the bond sale.

The Ministry of Finance published the 10-year result at 12:35pm Tokyo time, 11:35pm ET. The coupon, the bond's stated yearly interest rate, is 3.1%. The bond is issued October 7 and matures September 20, 2036. A 10-year yield is what that government pays to borrow for a decade.

The price competition, from that result:

- Bids, the money offered: 7,401.1 billion yen.
- Accepted: 1,966.1 billion yen.
- Bids for each yen accepted, from those two amounts: 3.76.
- Average yield: 3.101%.

Bloomberg's comparison with earlier sales:

- Previous sale: 3.29 bids per yen accepted.
- Average over the past year: 3.21.

Tuesday was above both. Buyers showed up at a yield just over 3.1%.

A second round, for the dealers allowed into it, was set for 2:00pm Tokyo time at that average price. That is 1:00am ET, so it is only starting. It is not in the figures above. About an hour and a half after that result, Tokyo's stock gain was still there.

The US 10-year Treasury yield is the rate Washington pays to borrow for a decade. It feeds mortgage rates and company loans.

- US 10-year Treasury yield, Monday's close: 5.31%, up 0.03 percentage point from Friday's 5.28%.

The yield finished higher. A higher borrowing cost is not a gift to stock prices. That is why Tokyo's gain does not, by itself, read as a broad move into riskier assets.

Friday's jobs report is why Monday's Nikkei surge happened. The Bureau of Labor Statistics counts jobs added or lost across the country. The report came Friday, October 2.

- Jobs added in September: 29,000.
- The widely reported estimate: about 90,000.
- Unemployment rate: 4.2%.

Hiring was much slower than expected. That cooled bets on another increase in the Federal Reserve's key short-term rate. Reuters, citing CME Group's FedWatch tool on Monday, put the odds this way. The tool reads them from futures tied to that rate.

- Chance of an increase at the October 27-28 meeting: 24%.
- A week earlier, in that same report: 70%.

On September 16 the Fed raised the target range, the band for that rate, by a quarter of a percentage point.

- Target range: 3.75% to 4.00%.

The odds of an October increase fell. Monday's 10-year yield rose.

US stock futures trade overnight. They hint at the next regular session, and they are not the stock indexes. Each change is since Monday's close.

- Dow futures: 51,625.00, +67.00 points / +0.13% since Monday's close.
- S&P 500 futures: 7,833.50, +7.25 points / +0.09% since Monday's close.
- Nasdaq-100 futures: 31,339.75, +22.00 points / +0.07% since Monday's close.
- Russell 2000 futures: 2,867.20, -0.60 points / -0.02% since Monday's close.

The Dow futures lead the four, at 0.13%. The small-company contract is the only decline. None of the four is close to Tokyo's 0.78%. That is not a market taking Tokyo's bid.

Europe is not a live vote. These are Monday's finishes.

- FTSE 100 (UK): 10,498, +35.94 points / +0.34% in Monday's session, now closed.
- DAX (Germany): 25,254, +23.01 points / +0.09% in Monday's session, now closed.
- CAC 40 (France): 7,834.10, -63.09 points / -0.80% in Monday's session, now closed.

Paris was the only decline in that list. None of the three is a read on Tuesday afternoon in Tokyo.

The clock, Eastern time:

- 2:30am: Tokyo's regular close.
- About 3:00am: London, Frankfurt, and Paris open.
- 4:00am: Hong Kong closes.
- Tuesday, October 6, 1:00pm: the Treasury auctions $58 billion of new 3-year notes.
- Wednesday, October 7, 1:00pm: $39 billion of 10-year notes. 2:00pm: minutes of the Fed's September 15-16 meeting, the detailed notes of that rate decision.
- Thursday, October 8: Shanghai reopens. 1:00pm: $22 billion of 30-year bonds.
- Wednesday, October 28, 2:00pm: the Fed's next rate decision.

What would knock down the read that the US open is not following Tokyo: S&P 500 futures rising on the scale of this Nikkei gain before 9:30am ET. What would say the afternoon bid itself failed: a Tokyo close back under 70,000. What would leave the quiet read in place: those US futures still near these levels at 9:30am ET.

The number that decides the open is where S&P 500 futures sit at 9:30am ET. The key risk is time. Tokyo is still in session, and an overnight move can fade, or flip, before the US regular open.

text:
Same week, three separate stories. 
An overview :
Easy to mash them into a “reset.” 
They are not one.

Seoul, 3 October. XRP Asia launched at the Grand Hyatt during Korea Blockchain Week. 

XRP Seoul, hosted by XRPL Korea with Ripple as title sponsor, pulled more than 5,000 people. 

The new body is backed by Ripple and the XRP Ledger Foundation, based in Singapore, and run by Sabrina Tachdjian, who used to handle fintech and payments at the Hedera Foundation. 

The brief is practical: 
developer education, hackathons, startup grants, and backing the existing Korea and Japan communities while building others across Asia-Pacific. Woori, KakaoBank, K Bank, Kyobo Securities, Meritz and Jeonbuk were in the room on cross-border payments and tokenized deposits. Jeonbuk already uses Ripple Payments for corporate remittances, REPLACING multi-day SWIFT windows. 

That is a live rail. 
It is not the same as the panel signing up to settle in XRP, and neither Woori nor KakaoBank announced they had joined XRP Asia or deployed the ledger.

Washington moved because Congress didn’t. 

The CLARITY Act stalled in the Senate last month, so on 5 October CFTC Chair Mike Selig put Regulation CTX and Regulation CAM out at Fordham Law. 

CTX covers crypto transactions done with margin, leverage or financing. 
CAM is a new venue category for exchanges that want to offer that to retail under one federal setup instead of a stack of state money-transmitter licenses. 

Reuters noted proof-of-reserves and anti-manipulation requirements. 

No fixed leverage cap, but a leveraged product would still need CFTC staff clearance. 

Selig was plain about the hole: the agency cannot force ordinary spot trading onto its platforms. 

That part of CLARITY needed a law. 
This is an opt-in lane, written because the bill failed, and he said they would keep going with or without Congress.
 
The products are narrower than the headlines. 

On 2 October the SEC approved Cboe BZX rule SR-CboeBZX-2026-065, Release 34-106577, so Volatility Shares can list six 3x daily funds: 
Bitcoin, Ether, gold, silver, crude oil and natural gas. 
Cboe filed on 10 August. 
No public comments. 
US crypto funds had been stuck at 2x — Volatility Shares already runs BITX and ETHU — after staff pushed back in December 2025 on anything above that, and waved off 5x filings in March. 
These new ones target three times the daily move of first- and second-month futures, with cash as collateral, not coins in a vault. 

Tickers floated for the crypto pair include BITH and ETHK. 
They are not trading. 
The registration statement still has to go effective, and the order sets no date. 
Bloomberg’s Eric Balchunas called the listing a win for the issuer and a trading tool, not an investment.

Payments talks in Asia, with one bank already off SWIFT. 

Rules written because the Senate bill died. 
Triple-leverage futures funds one filing away from a US listing. That’s the week. 
No switch flipped.
The rails are real. 
A promised revaluation is not.
Watch who is moving money. Ignore who is only on stage.

text:
Most startup advice is noise. This isn’t.

Elon Musk stood at Stanford in 2003, 32 years old, PayPal just sold, SpaceX barely a year old.

No rockets had flown. No Tesla. Just a guy who had already built and exited twice.

He skipped the pep talks. He walked through what actually worked.

Zip2 started because the internet was still invisible to most VCs. He deferred Stanford and bet the company would return cash fast.

PayPal grew without ads. The feature no one cared about became the product. Viral loops beat marketing budgets.

He sold it, then pointed the money at space because the existing industry had stopped trying.

Rockets were expensive because no one had redesigned the process. Parallel development, fewer suppliers, first principles on cost.

He called out China and Russia as the real competition, not the U.S. status quo.

SpaceX’s target was simple: make orbital launch cheap enough that Mars stops being science fiction.

He told the room a degree is optional. Execution is not.

Back-office systems at PayPal were a mess until they weren’t. Details compound.

eBay made offers before the deal closed. Timing and leverage matter more than perfect terms.

The lecture runs under 50 minutes. No slides full of frameworks. Just the sequence of decisions that turned early internet bets into rockets.

Watch it once. Then ask which of your current assumptions would still survive that room. https://t.co/JAVPXqfHgY

text:
Former US President, Jimmy Carter’s intervention helped Uganda drive guinea worm from 126,369 cases in 1992 to just two cases by April 2001, before the country recorded its last indigenous case in July 2003.

A 1992 national search found cases in 2,667 villages, with nearly 95 percent concentrated in Kitgum, Kotido and Moroto, where war and limited access to safe water forced communities to drink from ponds.

Carter offered President Yoweri Museveni assistance against the disease in 1990. Cloth filters, case containment and other measures helped reduce indigenous cases to 92 by 2000 and two between November 2000 and April 2001.

During a June 2001 visit, Carter also inspected Sasakawa Global 2000 farming projects east of Kampala, where 5,000 mainly women-led households had tripled maize, rice and millet yields.

He also pressed Museveni on the 1999 Nairobi agreement with Sudan’s Omar al-Bashir, which he had helped mediate to end support for each other’s rebels.

text:
Amazon blocked Meta from buying for shoppers. Can Meta break through the wall?👇
⠀
Meta ($META) launched Muse on September 8, 2026.
⠀
This is the company's first standalone personal AI agent.
⠀
Users can use it through a dedicated app, a web interface, and WhatsApp.
⠀
The service initially launched for U.S. adults 18 and older, and has since expanded to Canada.
⠀
By October 3, CNBC reported Muse was rolling out shopping features.
⠀
They let users ask the assistant to find products by brand, price, and availability, browse recommendation lists, and check out through the app or website.
⠀
Users can choose to open the retailer's website after clicking a list, or open it inside the Muse app and check out with the agent.
⠀
When they choose agent checkout, Muse prepares the checkout flow in advance, shows an 'approval card' with order details for the user to confirm, and requires the user to give access to email, full name, and address.
⠀
Payment can go through Link by Stripe, Meta's payment partner, or Shopify ($SHOP) Shop Pay; the user has to link Shop Pay; Link creates one-time cards to hide the real card number.
⠀
Meta says PayPal ($PYPL) has been announced as a payment provider for Muse, but it is not live yet.
⠀
-----
⠀
🔴 Follow me on X: @rich_compass
⠀
U.S. stock, crypto, and technical analysis
⠀
-----

▋ The fast lane arrives but not all connectors are live
⠀
Meta announced on September 23 that it built a group of retail partners for the Muse platform, including Walmart ($WMT), Gap ($GAP), Sephora, Expedia ($EXPE), Wayfair ($W), Best Buy ($BBY), and others, and called it the 'official fast lane' for the Muse agent platform.
⠀
CNBC noted that not all of what it called 'connectors' are live.
⠀
Ticketmaster, which was included in the partner list, said final purchases still happen inside its own secure marketplace.
⠀
CNBC quoted its spokesperson as saying consumers keep full control over purchase decisions.
⠀
Crypto Briefing reported that Muse runs on the Muse Spark 1.3 model, has a 1 million token context window, and operates in a sandbox environment Meta calls Muse Secure VM to protect user data and financial information.
⠀
Zuckerberg previously teased a future model codenamed 'Watermelon' that The Information reported Meta planned for October, but as of October 6 it has not been officially released nor confirmed as Spark 1.3's direct successor.
⠀
Muse has a free plan, and paid plans are Power at $20 per month and Maximum at $100 per month.

▋ Amazon keeps its block up after the credential dispute
⠀
Amazon ($AMZN) started blocking Meta's Muse from completing purchases on Amazon on the evening of September 20, 2026.
⠀
It deployed an anti-bot wall, so Muse users on iOS, Android, and WhatsApp were cut off when they tried to reach Amazon, and a popup appeared saying they violated Amazon's terms of use.
⠀
CNBC reported that Amazon blocked Muse from buying products on Amazon's website because of a terms of service violation, and Amazon said Muse stores customer credentials and scrapes account data.
⠀
The e-commerce giant stated that Meta never notified it or got authorization before Muse accessed https://t.co/d2eVnDxN9g and operated inside customer accounts.
⠀
More critically, it pointed out that Muse did not identify itself as an automated agent while browsing; Amazon alleged Muse retrieves and stores customer credentials, raising privacy concerns.
⠀
Meta clarified that user login credentials are kept in isolated secure storage, and the Muse model itself cannot see passwords or payment methods.
⠀
Despite the clarification, the block remains in place.
⠀
A company spokesperson said third-party apps that buy for customers should work openly and respect whether a service provider wants to take part.
⠀
GeekWire reported that Amazon asked Meta to remove Amazon from that experience.
⠀
Both companies are currently in direct talks about the matter.
⠀
When asked whether it is considering legal action, the company declined to comment.

▋ Zuckerberg wants a sales cut but keeps the rate quiet
⠀
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said at Meta Connect that the company will charge a small fee on Muse transactions.
⠀
Yahoo Finance reporter Daniel Howley reported Zuckerberg told developers at Meta Connect 'We believe that Muse will make you money', and said Meta is backing that up first by offering lots of free tokens, with long-term profit expected to come from small fees on transactions.
⠀
On The Verge 'Sources' podcast, Zuckerberg told Alex Heath that Meta will 'take a very small cut of whatever the transaction is', with the cost borne by merchants that transact with users.
⠀
Ainvest's analysis said Zuckerberg did not provide a cut number, 'very small' is not a specific number, and Muse had no transaction volume, no reported revenue item, and was only available in the U.S. at the time.
⠀
The analysis noted users themselves do not pay; the cost is borne by businesses on the other side of the transaction.
⠀
Analysts note transaction fees are expected to be one of Muse's long-term monetization paths, but there is no indication Meta will abandon subscriptions, as it explores subscriptions, transaction fees, and enterprise services together.
⠀
Zuckerberg said at Meta Connect that Meta expects to profit by charging small fees on transactions that agents complete for users, and will first offer lots of free tokens to attract users.
⠀
In fact, Meta's second-quarter revenue was $60.8 billion, with $59.4 billion from advertising, while Muse currently has no ads at all.
⠀
Yahoo Finance, citing Benzinga, reported Meta President and Vice Chair Dina Powell McCormick said on CNBC's 'Mad Money' with host Jim Cramer that Meta is evaluating multiple ways to monetize Muse, including transaction fees and paid subscriptions.
⠀
She explained on the show: 'Muse is saving a lot of people money right now, so we are thinking about, as Mark said last week, the possibility of charging when we save you money.'
⠀
During the interview, she also launched Muse for small businesses to help owners manage cash flow, inventory, website design, and customer communications.
⠀
Behind that push is Meta's 3.6 billion Family daily active people (DAP) and 200 million small businesses, with lab AI products aimed at making the core business stronger.
⠀
Addressing security concerns, McCormick noted Meta delayed Muse's launch by 30 days to make sure the product was safe, encrypted, and error-free before launch.
⠀
In addition, Meta opened the connector platform and continues to expand its Meta Business Agent—launched back in June—which helps businesses answer questions, recommend products, book appointments, and qualify leads.
⠀
The article said the biggest signal is the Shopify partnership, which lets Muse browse merchant catalogs and complete purchases with Shop Pay.
⠀
On their own, these features do not bring in much revenue, but they add supply of goods and services for the agent to take a cut from.

▋ Behind outside agent blocks, Amazon guards ad revenue and direct relationships
⠀
GeekWire reported Amazon has huge business interests: beyond its flagship e-commerce site, Amazon generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, and that business depends on people browsing its pages and seeing sponsored products.
⠀
Over the past year, Amazon has tried to keep outside agents away from its website, including suing Perplexity over the Comet browser and moving to block shopping agents from Google ($GOOGL) and OpenAI.
⠀
Amazon's own agentic shopping feature Buy for Me identifies itself and lets brands opt out.
⠀
In a related legal clash, the company won a preliminary injunction against Perplexity in March, but the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals overturned it on August 4, ruling that users rather than the AI company accessed computers under federal anti-hacking laws.
⠀
While a rehearing request was denied on September 10, the ruling still leaves Amazon a path to pursue claims based on contract and terms of service.
⠀
An AI Business Review analysis pointed out the block weakens Muse's core value proposition, because shopping is the key use case for AI agents.
⠀
With eMarketer estimating Amazon accounted for about 38% of U.S. ecommerce sales in 2023, its catalog is difficult to replace.
⠀
The retail landscape has begun to divide: Walmart, Gap, Best Buy, and Shopify have embraced agentic shopping, while Amazon, Kohl's, and eBay impose restrictions, and brands like Tapestry allow browsing but limit direct transactions.
⠀
Overseas, while Amazon Marketplace is subject to the EU Digital Markets Act, current DMA rules do not explicitly mandate accepting unauthorized shopping agents, though differential treatment could trigger competition scrutiny.
⠀
The analysis noted regulatory attention could soon follow.

▋ Shopping inside the agent puts brand traffic at risk
⠀
Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia Darden School of Business who studies psychological responses to AI, told CNBC that pushing shopping into a single agentic shopping experience will intensify competition among shopping giants.
⠀
He said 'the real battlefield for Muse is among companies, and consumers are the prize', and 'whoever owns the agent owns the relationship with the shopper'.
⠀
CNN cited IDC analyst Francisco Jeronimo saying Meta has done a better job than other tech giants at showing consumers what Muse can do.
⠀
'Others have not promoted agent shopping as hard as Meta has through Muse, and I think that is the main difference,' he explained.
⠀
The network also quoted Kathryn Heinz, Expedia vice president of enterprise alliances and AI, saying Expedia chose to allow AI agents because it wants to 'show up wherever travelers search', and added that about two-thirds of Expedia's traffic comes from its own platforms.
⠀
Market reaction was swift: following the announcement, travel stocks faced re-evaluation, with shares of Expedia, Airbnb, and Booking experiencing temporary dips between 5% and 7%.
⠀
Yet agentic shopping brings broader friction: if purchases stay inside assistant apps, brand website traffic could drop alongside direct customer engagement.
⠀
Brands could also lose the ability to understand customer shopping habits or drive add-on purchases through in-app promotions and recommendations.
⠀
A Yahoo Tech analysis emphasized responsibility is a problem at the center of this dispute: if Muse places a wrong or fraudulent order, Amazon and its sellers bear the returns and disputes, rather than Meta.
⠀
Online restaurant reservation platform Resy also stated it 'currently does not allow unapproved third-party bots or agents' to access its service.
⠀
The platform temporarily locked a user's account after another assistant, Instinct, sent around 200 API requests per hour to monitor open tables.

▋ Dynamic pricing fears grow while Meta's platform governance faces scrutiny
⠀
CNBC cited a January survey from Morning Consult that found 59% of U.S. adults said price gouging is a 'major concern' when it comes to AI-driven dynamic pricing.
⠀
Seeking to reassure shoppers, Walmart CEO John Furner published an open letter promising not to use shoppers' personal information to run dynamic pricing on its website or shopping tools.
⠀
Still, Meta's broader record on privacy, child safety, and platform governance presents a high trust bar, following a court-approved multistate settlement of nearly $17 billion.

▋ Early downloads spike but the real test starts when free tokens run out
⠀
Crypto Briefing and Reuters reported the Muse app reached roughly 2.8 million downloads in its first two weeks, and surpassed 5 million cumulative downloads by late September.
⠀
Yahoo Finance cited Sensor Tower estimating DAU at roughly 560,000 on the app's eleventh day, while Ainvest noted the app hit the top of the Apple App Store within a week.
⠀
Cantor Fitzgerald analysts described Muse's early unit economics as 'subsidized'.
⠀
Download surges are typical for heavily promoted launches; the true retention test begins once free tokens run dry.
⠀
Meanwhile, Meta projects full-year 2026 total capital expenditures of $130 billion to $145 billion, with AI infrastructure as a primary driver.
⠀
On a trailing twelve months (TTM) basis, capital expenditures ran near $92 billion against $38.5 billion in free cash flow, which dropped 23%.
⠀
Analysts interpret that heavy spending as aggressive investment rather than structural deterioration.
⠀

text:
Honda Rewires Its India Plan With Tata Tech Deal: Japanese Automaker Aims to Cut Costs by Up to a Fifth and Halve Development Times, as Pressure From Rivals Forces a Rethink of Its Go-It-Alone Approach

The Tata Technologies Partnership
Honda Motor aims to cut costs by as much as a fifth and halve development times under its new partnership in India with Tata Technologies, according to two people familiar with the matter

In May, Tata Technologies said it was selected to develop vehicles for a Japanese automaker; it declined to name the partner, but the two people and another person familiar said it was Honda

Under the outsourcing agreement, Tata Technologies will develop cars for the Indian market, while Honda expects to see up to 20% in cost reductions and halve its development times from around five years at present

The partnership had been under discussion for about two years before being finalised, one of the people added

Honda's Wider Pressures
Honda is reeling from EV-related losses that it expects to exceed $12 billion

It is pivoting to gasoline-electric hybrids and slashing expenses

Last month, Reuters reported that it is seeking to cut more than $9 billion in costs over the next four years and has told suppliers to drastically reduce prices

Pressure from rivals is forcing the Japanese automaker to rethink its go-it-alone approach

The Supplier Deadlock
Honda decided to bring in Tata Technologies after the automaker's Japanese and Indian managers failed to agree on which suppliers to use for upcoming vehicles in India, two of the people said

Japanese managers wanted to retain established suppliers to ensure quality and consistency

Honda's India team pushed for greater use of local suppliers to lower costs and speed up development in the world's third-largest car market

Reuters could not determine how long the deadlock lasted, but it was enough to delay work on some products

All three sources declined to be identified because the information has not been made public; the cost-cutting targets and the internal deadlock are being reported for the first time

Honda's Response
Honda said it has not been able to offer a sufficient product line-up in India that allows customers "value for money" products

To that end, it was "redefining" its offerings in India and planned to introduce vehicles that strike a balance between quality and price

It denied there were disagreements between the Japanese and Indian teams over supplier selection

In a separate statement, Honda India said product development involved close collaboration between different teams, adding it was inaccurate to characterise collaborative discussions as disagreements

Tata Technologies did not respond to a request for comment

Core Theme 
Honda is turning to Tata Technologies to rebuild its India strategy, targeting up to 20% lower costs and development cycles cut from about five years to roughly half that, as heavy EV-related losses above $12 billion, a planned $9 billion cost-cutting drive and a stalled internal disagreement over Japanese versus local suppliers push it away from its go-it-alone approach; the outsourcing deal is meant to help Honda finally field "value for money" vehicles in the world's third-largest car market, though the company itself disputes that there was any disagreement between its teams.

Slide 4 is a PEG chart with a footnote that defines it as FY27 P/E divided by annualized FY26 to FY28 EPS growth.

That growth adjustment is the whole reason $JPM shows up at 2.76. I agree size and regulation matter. $JPM is a G-SIB with capital surcharges SOFI doesn’t carry and that justifies a different multiple on its own. It’s also why I didn’t stop at $JPM. SOFI had a lower PEG than $C, $BAC, $WFC and $TFC as well.

Now the broker vs asset manager point that you made. SoFi Invest runs through two registered entities. SoFi Securities is a FINRA member broker dealer that handles self directed active investing. SoFi Wealth is the SEC registered RIA behind robo and advisory.

Robinhood is set up the same way with Robinhood Financial as the broker dealer and Robinhood Asset Management as the RIA behind Robinhood Strategies. The BD and the RIA are separate registrations and both companies hold both.

I also said in my last post that SOFI and Robinhood get to their earnings through different business mixes. The comp was never about matching business lines but rather what the market pays for a similar expected growth rate.

Noto framed his own valuation the same way on our podcast when he tied a 1.1 PEG to a comparable group of financial services companies and fintechs.

On the bank question I never said SOFI isn’t a bank. Slide 3 is titled “A Tech Growth Profile Inside a Bank.” Slide 12 is “The Bank Charter Is the Engine.” The NIM, the deposit funding and the reserves held at the Fed are in the deck because of the charter and the slides say that directly.

My argument is about how to value a bank that the analyst consensus estimates have growing EPS 75% over the next two years. To be specific from the end of the 2026 fiscal year through the 2028 fiscal year. Whether it’s a bank was never in question.

SoFiUSD is where I think we agree more than you realize. The deck nor my discussion never compares SoFiUSD to anything Robinhood does with stablecoins. Deposits went from 78% of funding in 2023 to 93% in Q2 and management puts the savings versus warehouse funding at about $713 million a year. SOFI produced it's eleventh straight quarter of GAAP profitability in Q2 and that is a large portion of the bull case.

text:
And grok again about the running girls to Epstein:
No. There is no evidence that Trump sent girls from Mar-a-Lago to Epstein for sex. The documented recruiting ran the other way.
Virginia Giuffre, the main public accuser tied to the club, said she was working as a locker-room attendant in the Mar-a-Lago spa when Ghislaine Maxwell approached her. Maxwell noticed her reading a massage book, talked about anatomy, and offered work as a traveling masseuse for Epstein. That is her account in deposition and in her memoir: Maxwell hired her out of the spa. She did not say Trump handed her over. In the memoir she described meeting Trump once at the club, where her father also worked, and said he “couldn’t have been friendlier” and offered to help her find babysitting work. She did not accuse him of abuse.
Trump’s own later account matches the direction of that recruiting. In July 2025 he said Epstein “stole” spa staff, that people complained Epstein was taking employees, that he told Epstein to stop, and that he threw him out after it happened again. Asked if those employees were young women and if Giuffre was one of them, he said yes, and added that she had no complaint about the club. Mar-a-Lago records put the ban around October 2007, years after Giuffre was recruited in 2000. Former spa staff have also described Epstein exposing himself and pressuring employees, including an 18-year-old beautician whose complaint reached managers.
The emails Democrats released in November 2025 do not say he supplied girls either. Epstein wrote to Michael Wolff that a Mar-a-Lago worker (the White House identified her as Giuffre) “was the one that accused Prince Andrew,” and then: “Of course he knew about the girls as he asked ghislaine to stop.” In another note Epstein wrote that Trump spent hours at his house with a victim, “never got a massage,” and was “the dog that hasn’t barked.” Those are Epstein’s unverified words. Read straight, they claim Trump knew something and told Maxwell to stop, not that he was sending girls over.
What does not count as evidence: an anonymous FBI tip, briefly posted and then pulled in the 2026 document release, claiming Trump hosted “calendar girl” parties and auctioned children. Snopes and the Justice Department treated that as an unverified tip with no supporting evidence. A separate civil allegation that Epstein once brought a teen to Mar-a-Lago and told Trump “this is a good one” is an unproven claim in a lawsuit about Epstein and Maxwell, not a finding that Trump furnished anyone.
So the record shows Epstein and Maxwell poaching from the spa, Trump later saying he ordered it stopped and banned Epstein, and the best-known victim from that spa never accusing him of sending her or of abusing her. It does not show him running girls from the club to Epstein
